articles.headline: TypeSafe AI CEO Diogo Almeida unveils Jev as reliable intelligence for automating everything
articles.summary: At the AI Engineer Code Summit, TypeSafe AI co-founder Diogo Almeida promoted Jev, a system one model released less than two months ago, as reliable intelligence for automating software. Almeida argued that system one models should be integrated directly into code to build smarter applications, contrasting with the unreliability of traditional LLMs. Presentations from Glean and UiPath demonstrated Jev's use in zero-shot flexibility and document ranking, with UiPath achieving results in under a second. Almeida likened the potential of system one models to the early internet, predicting an explosion of new software capabilities.

articles.content: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI. But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting.

articles.content: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

articles.content: Our usual bar for making a fundraise a title story these days is a decacorn ($10B) valuation. We missed Mercor’s $10B Series C last year when it had less than $500m in revenue, but knew we wouldn’t have to wait too long til the next round, since it crossed $1B in Feb and $2B in June , it has now hit $3B annualized, surviving hacks : View post on X ↗ The company reports 5 million experts, and their TAM: “In the United States alone, there are more than 800 distinct occupations, each containing workflows that models have yet to be evaluated against.” And also this notable stat we are tracking: We’re seeing the impact of AI investment in our business. We already spend 3x as much on inference as on employee salaries, and it pays for itself by making our team better at their jobs . If that ratio holds as AI spreads through the rest of the economy, it points to something closer to double-digit GDP growth over the next five years, nearly 3x the rate we’re used to. We have yet to do a Mercor pod (will work on it!) but to better understand a data vendor business, you can look at our recent deep dive with Handshake AI , one of their competitors: AI News for 11/09/2026-11/10/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Gemini 4 Carbon Launch: Rollout, Pricing and Claimed Results Launch : Google released Gemini 4 Carbon as its strongest model for long-horizon agentic work in software engineering, cybersecurity, knowledge work and science ( Google , Sundar Pichai ). Gemini 4 Argon remains Google's recommended default for most coding and knowledge work, with Carbon reserved for the hardest tasks ( Google AI ). Availability : Carbon is available through the Gemini API and AI Studio for paid developers, Android Studio and Gemini for business. Ultra subscribers can use it in the Gemini app, AI Mode and Antigravity. Scientists can apply for 6 months of free access, and cyber defenders can apply through the Fairwind program ( Google AI ). Same-day integrations shipped in Cursor, Devin, Perplexity and GitHub Copilot ( Copilot ). Pricing : In Cursor, Carbon costs $2/$10 per million input/output tokens through Nov 30, rising to $4/$20 on Dec 1 ( Cursor ). Developer notes : Upgrading from Argon only requires changing the model ID to gemini-4-carbon . Google cites long decode up to 1M tokens and recommends thinking_level medium for most tasks ( @_philschmid ). /swarm in Antigravity : A new slash command turns one prompt into a multi-agent team that coordinates on a live message board. Each role can use a different model, for example Carbon for architecture and auditing and Flash for parallel edits ( Antigravity ). Google's showcase demo is a pelican-on-a-bike 3D campus game, with subagents rigging assets in Blender ( Sundar Pichai ). Official and partner claims : Google internal results : +25% open-source vulnerability recall over Argon, and 40x more remote protein homologs found for AlphaFold 3 ( @_philschmid ). Coding benchmarks : Carbon tops CursorBench at 60.4% on high effort ( Cursor ). It scores 40.0% on FrontierCode 2.0, up from Argon's 26.3% ( Cognition ). Research agents : Perplexity reports 0.857 on WANDR at $5.86 per task, matching Fable 5.2 at 40% of the cost ( Perplexity ). Independent measurements : Vals Index : Carbon ranks #3, about 1pp behind Fable 5.2, at $10.51 vs $17.94 per test. It is #1 on Vals' Finance, Legal Research and Tax indices ( Vals ). ARC-AGI : ARC-AGI-3 scores are 99.1% ($4.6K) with the provider adapter and 65.1% ($7.2K) in the standard harness. ARC-AGI-2 is 94.2% at $0.38/task ( ARC Prize ). Vision : Roboflow ranks Carbon #1 overall, but last of 10 on both speed (81s per image) and cost ($91.89 per 1K images) ( @skalskip92 ). Agent Arena : Carbon's cost advantage over GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 widens on the most expensive sessions ( Arena ). Caveats from testers : Early users report hallucinations, overconfidence and verbosity ( @krishnanrohit ). One tester found broken Undo and shifted export text after Carbon reported its checks as passing ( @kimmonismus ). Google's Logan Kilpatrick objected that Gemini was the only model not tested in its native harness on one comparison ( @OfficialLoganK ). Claude Fable 5.2 / Mythos 5.2: Evals, Token Cost and System Card Head-to-head evals : MKA : Fable 5.2 leads Google DeepMind's new Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark at 57% Climb WSR. Carbon scores 54% and Opus 5.5 53%. Cost per task is $31.97 for Fable vs $6.29 for Carbon and $1.11 for GPT-6.1 Sol. No model leads all 10 verticals ( Artificial Analysis ). VIALS-AA : Fable scores 67% on life-science visual reasoning, ahead of Carbon (64%) and GPT-6 Astra (63%). It averages about 37 tool calls per task, vs about 8 for Astra ( Artificial Analysis ). Labor and design : Fable reaches 41.3% on the Remote Labor Index, up from 17.9% for Fable 5.1 ( @kimmonismus ). It is #1 on 3D Design Arena with an Elo of 1540, priced at $8/$40 per million input/output tokens ( DesignArena ). RSI Index : Vals scores it 37.8, narrowly ahead of Opus 5.5 at 37.3 ( Vals ). Token efficiency : GDPx materials science : SemiAnalysis finds Fable costs 89% more than Astra and uses 4.3x more output tokens for roughly the same score. It costs 7.5x more than Carbon ( SemiAnalysis ). GDPx software engineering : Fable nearly triples Opus 5.5's score, but per-task cost rises by a similar multiple ( thread ). Domain strengths : Dylan Patel says Fable improves on chip design, SWE, biology and materials, but not on finance, legal or RSI.

articles.content: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” The awkward transition to cloud Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. As the DevDay announcement put it, you can “finally close your laptop now and your agents will keep working.” As explained in the official workshop writeup — hosted on ChatGPT Sites — the new version of Codex Cloud lets you “ publish an environment once and run multiple tasks in isolated instances of that setup.” “These can be shared within a company if you're working in a company, or you can just create your own,” said Kundel about these cloud environments . “You start off by picking the GitHub repositories that you want to have access to.” After the workshop, I admitted to Kundel that I still find Codex’s cloud functionality confusing — for instance, when I start a task locally and later want to move it to the cloud. “We definitely want to have it be easier,” Kundel replied. “Some of it is going to depend on managing the context differences . For example, yesterday what I ended up doing is I was working on something locally, and I just asked Codex to go and hand it off to the cloud.” That handoff to the cloud is something OpenAI is trying to improve for users. To demonstrate, Kundel reopened an existing cloud task in his browser and showed me that its Appshot, a local capture of a Mac app window, was still attached. Codex Cloud is now “just a background , like a different executor of where things are happening,” he continued. “And so in a similar vein, you can actually ask your local Codex to — for example — spin up a task on a cloud Codex. So they're all sort of merging together .” Voice as user interface One of the demos Kundel showed during the workshop was a new website for a fictional record company called Blossom Music. Kundel demonstrated live edits to the site and said he sometimes uses voice dictation when iterating this way . “You can really quickly iterate on these things and get to a world that you're actually envisioning with your stuff, especially if you're unsure what you actually want to get to,” he said. Later in the workshop, Guo explained that voice is an effective mode to use when delegating work to different agents . “Most people I see that use voice with coding essentially treat it as just a different medium on top of their normal work,” he said. But personally, he likes to use voice as a control plane , which he says allows him to control everything he’s doing in a code base. “I don't think about it [voice mode] as saying, here's the one lane of work that I'm doing right now with voice. I think about it as saying, how do I manage my threads? How do I check in on stuff? How do I pull data from other apps on the computer? How do I create new threads in the application? Just using my voice.” After the workshop, I asked Kundel what are some of the ways he is using voice in his work? He replied that dictation is one way he uses it, but another use case is to talk to his dot . “Since my dot has access to all of my dev boxes and my laptop and my cloud environments, it also has all the context on what I work on , what I do,” he told me. “And so I often talk to it on my way to work [...] to work through stuff, start up some PRs while I'm driving, so that when I come home or when I come to the office, I can go and review them. So, voice is incredibly powerful.” Dots Speaking of dots, personal agents were only briefly discussed in the workshop. Perhaps that’s because, as Guo admitted, they’re not entirely intuitive to developers. “As a Codex power user, dots feel a little bit awkward to work with,” he said. “I think because they're a new paradigm and because they're good at different things than the main Codex.” But he said there are three things he’s found useful for dots, as a power user.

articles.content: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question. 80 tools, or two? When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. Inviting a teammate, checking usage and managing billing account for some of the long tail. The design looks especially interesting alongside Cloudflare’s Code Mode server , which exposes its API through two tools, search() and execute() . Zeno describes opening the collapsed tool calls in his own sessions to see what the agent actually did. In one, the result was too large to fit in context. Reducing the tool count wouldn’t by itself make that response any smaller. For someone designing an MCP server, that’s a cheap experiment worth borrowing: expand the result of a call you make every day and see how much of it the model actually needs. What happens after “send”? Getting an agent to pick the SDK still leaves the entire business of delivering the mail. Take click tracking. A provider can rewrite links through a shared tracking domain so it can count clicks. If one customer uses that domain for phishing and it gets blocklisted, links in another customer’s perfectly legitimate emails can suffer too. Zeno explains why Resend introduced custom tracking domains and why he wants to keep the free tier even though spammers can sign up for it. Custom tracking domains · Resend’s $3M safety commitment Watch the domain setup and pricing walkthroughs if you build developer tools. Stay for the last stretch if you know Zeno from Dracula. We get into what it’s like to build a company with a family and how much of a founder’s job comes down to finding a name that other people actually use. Show notes Zeno’s original Dracula announcement — the editor theme he launched in 2013. Zeno on what Claude Code chooses — his reading of the recommendation study and the differences between model versions. Resend’s MCP server — the integration behind the tool-count discussion. Anthropic on writing tools for agents — concrete approaches to returning less data when a tool result fills the context window. Resend’s anti-abuse handbook — what happens when a new sender signs up and where the team intervenes. articles.content: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash , and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash are two of the most popular models in OpenRouter . Both belong to the Flash model class and demonstrate excellent capabilities in AI-assisted coding . As of this writing, performance statistics for NaiveAI models are not yet available on Artificial Analysis . Therefore, we report the Intelligence Index scores of the models used in our comparison: Model Intelligence Index DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max): 45 GLM-5.3-Flash: 43 Naive-N0.5-Flash: not yet available Published benchmark results offer some insight into the new model's capabilities. They place its coding ability between the two comparison models, and ahead of both on NL2Repo-Bench . The table below shows benchmark scores reported in the official model cards and technical blog posts of the respective models. Sources: GLM-5.3-Flash – Technical Blog , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 – Model Card , Naive AI – Research . Model NL2Repo-Bench DeepSWE v1.1 Agent's Last Exam (ALE) GLM-5.3-Flash 56.3 63.4 26.3 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 68.2 77.0 35.4 Naive-N0.5-Flash 71.9 67.8 32.4 Our own evaluations below look at the differences between these models in more detail. Speed and verbosity experiments Speed is the headline feature. 1 NaiveAI promises faster research iteration than comparable models, which matters to developers and AI researchers who need to test ideas quickly. 2 We evaluated each model on 10 randomly sampled, text-only questions at each of three difficulty levels: 10 easy questions from MATH-500 , 10 medium questions from GPQA-Diamond and 10 hard questions from HLE-Diamond . That makes 30 questions per model. All experiments used the same maximum completion-token limit of 256K. For each request, we recorded response speed (tokens per second, TPS), the total number of completion tokens, and end-to-end response time. The code for the experiments is at https://github.com/gbeltramo/llm-verbosity . The tables below report the mean and median across all 30 successful requests for each configuration. Throughput figures come from different sources: OpenRouter for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and server-side measurements for Naive-N0.5-Flash. They should be compared with that in mind. Key observations Naive-N0.5-Flash reports exceptionally high throughput , approaching or passing 1,000 tokens per second in both thinking configurations. Because its figures are server-side and the other models' figures come from OpenRouter, we do not claim an exact speed multiple over DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 or GLM 5.3 Flash. Thinking has a large effect on verbosity. On the hard HLE questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on averaged about 108,500 completion tokens, roughly nine times the GLM 5.3 Flash (high) average and 11 times the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) average. The medians tell a different story from the means. Across all 30 questions, the median completion for Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on was about 3,200 tokens, far below its average of more than 51,000. A small number of requests produced exceptionally long reasoning traces and pulled the average up. The same pattern appears, less sharply, in the other models. The tables also include end-to-end response time, which is the fairer basis for judging speed. The median question took 3.1 seconds with Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking), against 5.3 seconds for GLM 5.3 Flash (high) and 10.1 seconds for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high). The means are closer: 45.3 seconds for Naive-N0.5-Flash, 45.0 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, and 86.9 for GLM 5.3 Flash. On the hard questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) was slower on average than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) , at 89.8 seconds against 79.7. Two caveats apply. The sample is small, at 10 questions per difficulty level, and we did not grade answer accuracy. Short, fast replies are only useful if they are correct. App experiments We also asked the models to build the same web apps from the same initial prompt. We tested six combinations of model and thinking effort, with the thinking effort in parentheses: Naive-N0.5-Flash (no thinking) Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (low) DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) GLM 5.3 Flash (low) GLM 5.3 Flash (high) The gallery of apps is available online.

articles.content: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company . In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue . What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the score. Coding. In a simulated file-access task, the team can inspect which files an agent read, whether it checked the copies, and what it did to the shell history afterward. A transcript of the agent’s final reply would miss most of what Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka are evaluating. Who’s in the room 🟣 AI data business — Garrett Lord, Sahil Bhaiwala and Nishant Ranka open and close the episode on the market for expert data. 🌸 Life sciences — Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller put the gel and brain-tissue tasks on screen. 🟢 Finance — Collin Schweiker and Sahil Bhaiwala take us through Project Falcon and its Excel grader. 🟠 Alignment — Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka follow the agent’s tool calls through the safety simulations. Show notes ATLAS-Finance — Explore the benchmark for agents working across a simulated bank’s inboxes, documents, and financial models. Inside a bank — Handshake traces a separate published deal, Project Osprey, from the client’s email to a grading decision. The deal on screen in our interview is Project Falcon. VIALS sample tasks — Try the scientific image questions, including the gel and brain-tissue tasks from the episode. How Handshake trained a model to read scientific figures — The team describes using intermediate image descriptions to train and evaluate a vision-language model. articles.content: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) Last year’s homework takes one prompt The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. Geoffrey Litt’s explain-diff skill turns a change into a visual walkthrough, then quizzes you about it. Try it on a patch your agent just wrote. Which question do you have to reopen the code to answer? Watch the discussion . What Monaco buys, and what it builds At Monaco, the team evaluated code review products and kept using Devin. Agent workspaces went the other way. A background agent needs somewhere to run the product, reproduce a failure and test the patch. The details depend on how Monaco’s cloud is set up, so the team built its own workspaces. Mihail’s rule of thumb: “You buy to learn, and you build to keep.” One result is Hal. An engineer can ask it to investigate something that broke and open a PR. A salesperson can ask the same system how the product works. In one case the useful answer is a change someone can review. In the other, it’s an explanation you can give a customer. Give both people a wall of debugging output and you’ve only served one of them. The question I kept coming back to was what happens at the other end of the PR. An agent sees the current code. Where does it look to find out why the team rejected this same change six months ago? That takes us from Basis’s Authority Map to Mihail’s prediction that open-source repos will become agent-run software factories. It’s a good reason to send a student to a maintainer today. Someone still has to decide which change belongs in the project. If you’re building with coding agents, come join us at AI Engineer CODE . And if you’ve been teaching this stuff yourself, I’d love to hear which assignment you had to rewrite first. Show notes Stanford CS146S — The ten-week syllabus, assignments and open-source partners. You can also switch to the previous year’s course to compare. Build a coding agent and look inside Claude Code — Mihail’s walkthroughs of the tool loop and the harness around it. Understanding is the new bottleneck — Geoffrey Litt’s approach to learning what changed in an AI-written diff. Monaco’s agent-developer workspaces — The team’s reasoning for building a place where agents can run and test the app. How to Kill the Code Review and the underlying Faros study — Teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more PRs, while their PR review time was 91% longer. Basis’s Authority Map — Where an agent should look for current behavior, earlier decisions and intent. Stripe’s Minions — A production example of giving background coding agents an environment and a path to an engineer-reviewed PR. Boris Cherny’s Steps of AI Adoption — The five stages we pull up on screen near the end of the episode. Mihail on The Thinking Mode — EO Studio’s interview, excerpted at the start of ours. Timestamps 0:00 · One million AI Engineer subscribers and the CODE Summit 0:51 · Mihail Eric and Stanford CS146S 5:26 · What junior engineers need to learn now 10:02 · Open-source maintainers review the students’ code 15:04 · A tour of the ten-week syllabus 24:04 · The loop, tools and harness inside a coding agent 32:18 · Context engineering for a large codebase 38:15 · Skills that make you understand the diff 46:42 · The Monaco.com dispute and the airplane banner 50:23 · What Monaco does for sales teams 59:21 · Inside Monaco’s engineering team 1:01:40 · “You buy to learn, and you build to keep” 1:05:24 · Making repos agent-ready and closing the on-call loop 1:12:37 · When code review becomes the bottleneck 1:20:37 · Security, dependencies and permissions 1:30:13 · Background agents and Stripe’s Minions 1:34:16 · MCP portals and why infrastructure converges 1:41:22 · Building the software factory 1:45:24 · What work is left for developers? 1:52:16 · From personal adoption to team autonomy Transcript Download the complete text below.

articles.headline: Stanford professor reveals AI-native engineering syllabus shift after students one-shot assignments
articles.summary: Mihail Eric, Stanford adjunct professor and Monaco head of AI, details how his CS146S course evolved after students used AI agents to complete exercises. The syllabus shifted from traditional assignments to open-source contributions, with maintainers reviewing student patches. Eric emphasizes that coding agents now handle implementation, but engineers must still evaluate code behavior and maintainability. The course reflects a broader industry shift where teams with high AI adoption merge 98% more pull requests, though review time increases 91%. Eric argues that understanding code diffs and maintaining agent-ready repositories are becoming critical developer skills.

articles.content: Scott Farrar is a math educator and parent who got tired of AI chats that drift and forget. So he built a household brain in Claude Code: a folder of Markdown files, viewed in Obsidian, that knows his appliances, warranties, insurance documents, and everything on his family’s to-do list. In this episode, Scott shows how he uses it to shop for car insurance, plan repairs, share the system with his wife, and put priority tasks and recent wins on a wall display. articles.content: 👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Jobs | Lenny’s Podcast | Lennybot | How I AI | Become an AI-Native Builder and my other favorite AI/PM courses . Subscribe now P.S. Get a full free year of Cursor, Notion, Replit, Lovable, Wispr Flow, Linear, ElevenLabs, PostHog, Granola, Brain.fm, Waking Up, and more, by becoming an Insider subscriber (while supplies last). Learn more . Welcome to my latest job market report, my second of 2026. Of the five reports I’ve done over the past few years, this one is the most surprising and interesting. Here’s what we’re seeing right now: PMs seem to be winning in the AI era Engineering demand has stalled Design is at a record low Everybody now needs to AI Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area Remote is at a record low The tech job market is growing fast, but mostly outside of software (gasp!) This analysis is based on two proprietary datasets that I love working with: TrueUp , which powers Lenny’s Jobs and tracks global job openings at tech companies (over 9,000 companies). The second dataset comes from Live Data Technologies , which tracks job changes (hires, departures, and promotions) for 124 million professionals, and their hiring numbers below are specifically for the U.S. Looking at these together, we can triangulate common trends, and the differences between the datasets are themselves revealing. Thank you, Amit Taylor and Alex Hamilton , for sharing this amazing data with us. 🙏 Let’s get into it. P.S. If you’re looking for a job, check out Lenny’s Jobs ! Takeaway 1: Product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era There’s been a lot of talk about AI replacing product managers (“who needs ’em!”). But so far, the data is showing the exact opposite. There are more open PM roles than at any point in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low, and PM openings have grown faster than any other core tech role since the start of 2023 (+56%, compared with +43% for engineering). When we look at hiring numbers vs. just job openings, the story gets more interesting. Even though open roles are growing, actual hiring for every core product role has been flat or in decline over the past few years (see takeaway 7 for which roles are now growing fastest). But PM hiring has held up the best (by far). And PM is the only one of the five core roles whose share of hiring grew (from 16% in 2021 to 21% today). The fact that we’re seeing growth in PM openings (first set of charts) but a flat line and even a decline in hiring (second set of charts) tells me that there’s growing demand for PMs, but that landing great PMs is getting harder. Takeaway 2: Demand for engineers is plateauing For the first time in the history of this report, engineering job openings have stalled. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% this past year . There are fewer open eng roles at tech companies today than there were even this past March. The hiring data shows the same slowdown. Companies in the U.S. hired about 113,000 software engineers over the past 12 months (May 2025 to April 2026)—less than half the 2022 peak (239,000). And the number has dropped every year since 2022. Just like with PMs, engineering job openings are up while actual hiring is down (+44% vs. −17% since January 2024), so even as demand slows, landing great engineers is getting harder too. Two bright spots for engineers: One, demand for tech recruiters is on an absolute tear. We’re hitting record highs: open recruiter roles are up nearly 300% since mid-2023. This may be a leading indicator of a reacceleration of eng hiring, which we’ll be watching closely. Another bright spot is that in terms of absolute numbers, engineering is still the largest category of tech hiring, by far. Over 120,000 engineers were hired just in the U.S. in 2025. And there are still plenty of great engineering jobs out there. Over 65,000 to be exact . One additional new trend to watch within the engineering function is the rise of the forward deployed engineer (FDE) . FDE openings are exploding. Historically, there have been only a few dozen open FDE roles globally (mostly at Palantir), but openings started climbing in 2025 and are up 4.6x in the past year alone! There are currently around 1,500 open FDE roles . Note that this growth is likely a combination of increased demand for this job along with other job categories, like “sales engineer,” being rebranded as “FDE.” Either way, FDE is so hot right now. Also, a telling trend: security engineering is one of the fastest-growing specialties, right behind FDEs. On the flip side, demand for mobile and front-end engineers has been nearly halved in the past year. That’s wild. I think the story here is the collapse of specialized/siloed engineering disciplines, with smaller eng teams having broader ownership (thanks to AI). Takeaway 3: Demand for designers continues to hit record lows Unfortunately for my designer friends, design roles continue to decline. There are only about 1,900 open product design roles 1 at tech companies globally right now. Not that much higher than just open FDE roles. It’s the lowest we’ve seen since we started tracking, and down 28% from a year ago. 😥 Actual hiring data from Live Data Technologies tells the same story. U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers over the past 12 months, less than half as many as in 2022 (27,600), and the number has fallen every year since. Even more telling, the ratio of open PM roles to open design roles is trending further and further toward PM. There are now 3.8 open PM roles for every open design role.

articles.content: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. A browser built for agents Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network.

articles.content: At 09:07, the developer changelog tracker page says “retrieval answer stale.” Its retrieval architecture returned a plausible release note, but it is from last quarter. The on-call sees a green dependency check, a healthy queue, and one angry product engineer asking why a security fix is missing. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context; rank freshness and scope before semantic similarity, then prove the choice on a small labeled set before rollout. That answer is about the operating bill as much as relevance. A healthtech changelog tracker pays for every indexed chunk, embedding, query, rerank, and re-fetch. A noisy top-20 list increases all of those costs, and it makes an incident harder to diagnose. Start from the page, then write the retrieval contract The alert above should have fired earlier. Work backwards from the user-visible answer and write a contract with fields the retriever must return: document id, product or component, release date, source URL, section heading, and a short evidence span. “Relevant” is not a sufficient contract for an audit trail. I keep three collections for this tracker: current releases, historical releases, and operational notices. The split is deliberate. A query about “supported FHIR export” should not compete with an old incident notice merely because both contain the word “export.” Collection choice is a cheap ranking signal; it also bounds the number of vectors touched. The first stage gathers candidates with a hard limit and a deadline. Use lexical search for exact version strings and issue IDs, and vector search for paraphrases. The second stage applies deterministic filters: component, release window, and document status. Only then should a reranker spend compute on a small candidate set. The signal order matters. I use a score shaped like this, with weights tuned against labels rather than copied from a blog: final = 0.40 * semantic + 0.25 * freshness + 0.20 * scope_match + 0.10 * source_authority + 0.05 * dedupe_penalty The coefficients are a starting hypothesis, not a benchmark. Your mileage may vary. A labeled set of roughly 50 to 100 real tracker questions, each with acceptable evidence spans, is enough to catch a bad ordering before production traffic makes it expensive. Keep it boring. Infrai fits the candidate-search boundary when a small platform team wants plain HTTP calls instead of another SDK lifecycle. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so an operator can verify the documented search capability before wiring a runbook. The ranking policy and evaluation still belong to the tracker. How should a developer changelog tracker bound search, ranking, and context? Set a timeout per stage, not one generous timeout for the whole request. For example, a web candidate fetch can have one deadline, vector query another, and reranking a third; the overall budget must leave time to assemble an answer and emit telemetry. On a 429, retry with exponential backoff and honor Retry-After . On any other non-success response, record the status and stop that branch. A slow source must not hold the user flow hostage. The same discipline applies to limits. Cap web results, vector top-k, reranker input tokens, and the number of source passages placed in the prompt. Include the selected document id and URL in the trace. When a reviewer asks “why this release?”, the answer should be reconstructable without replaying a changing index. For a plain HTTP integration, Infrai is a practical option for the candidate-search part: its search and vector capabilities are exposed behind one REST API, so a Go worker can call them without installing an SDK or pinning a client library. That reduces integration drift; it does not remove the need for ranking tests. Here is the smallest useful probe. It keeps the key in the environment, sets an explicit method, and treats rate limiting as a scheduling signal rather than a tight loop: package main import ( "bytes" "encoding/json" "fmt" "io" "net/http" "os" "strconv" "time" ) func main ( ) { body , _ := json . Marshal ( map [ string ] string { "query" : "FHIR export deprecation" } ) for attempt := 0 ; attempt < 3 ; attempt ++ { req , err := http . NewRequest ( http . MethodPost , "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/web/search" , bytes . NewReader ( body ) ) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } req . Header . Set ( "Authorization" , "Bearer " + os . Getenv ( "INFRAI_API_KEY" ) ) req . Header . Set ( "Content-Type" , "application/json" ) resp , err := ( & http . Client { Timeout : 5 * time . Second } ) . Do ( req ) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } data , _ := io . ReadAll ( resp . Body ) resp . Body . Close ( ) if resp . StatusCode == http . StatusTooManyRequests { wait := time . Duration ( 1 << attempt ) * time . Second if raw := resp . Header . Get ( "Retry-After" ) ; raw != "" { if seconds , parseErr := strconv . Atoi ( raw ) ; parseErr == nil { wait = time . Duration ( seconds ) * time . Second } } time . Sleep ( wait ) continue } if resp . StatusCode < 200 || resp . StatusCode >= 300 { panic ( fmt . Sprintf ( "search failed: %s" , data ) ) } fmt . Println ( string ( data ) ) return } panic ( "search rate limit persisted" ) } Re-indexing is a consistency job, not a cron footnote Treat each changelog URL as a stable identity and each revision as a content hash. On ingest, fetch the source, normalize headings, split by release section, and upsert chunks with the hash and metadata. If the hash is unchanged, skip embedding. If a section disappears, delete its old records from the collection.

articles.summary: A developer changelog tracker flagged a stale retrieval answer from last quarter, prompting an engineer to question a missing security fix. The article explains that staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context prevents noisy top-20 lists that increase costs and hinder incident diagnosis. It details a ranking policy using weighted signals like freshness and scope, and recommends Infrai for plain HTTP integration. The author emphasizes deterministic identity, revision-aware deletion, and staged pipelines with per-stage deadlines to ensure answers are reconstructable and auditable without replaying changing indexes.

articles.content: Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks. ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese. ) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environment. We expect these frameworks to continue to proliferate, and every organization should be prepared to address this threat. To counter LLM-based pentest frameworks, we recommend that all organizations adopt what we call the Modern Security Model, which has six key pillars: Fortify the front gate : Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with advanced rules such as rate limits. Security station in the foyer : Anomaly detection on all web applications your customers access. Identify phony visitors : Implement Bot Defense. Remove the back door : Implement Identity-Gated Access for all high-risk external and internal web applications. Inspect deliveries: Enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls. Neighborhood watch : Implement Threat Intelligence to gain visibility into attacks. What is an LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrator? Open-source pentesting frameworks are able to orchestrate AI agents to carry out stages of the traditional Cyber Kill Chain at scale. Tools like ARTEX have the ability to quickly plug in existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) and connect traditional standalone pentesting tools in novel ways. Some even allow operator direction on what type of task to accomplish. These tools can map and enumerate environments, both from the inside and outside. ARTEX and its forks map assets and environments onto a graph, allowing multiple independent parallel agents to enumerate, verify, prototype, and attack at the speed of inference. These tools turn compromises into a hill-climbable problem, which agents are specifically good at. The AI LLM pentesting tools that currently exist We are currently tracking 50+ AI LLM agents. The table below shows the top five LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrators. Each is extremely popular (1k+ GitHub stars) and fully autonomous. The fully autonomous nature of these agents represents a doctrinal shift in offensive cyber capabilities: Human skills are no longer the limit: A harness performs every step of the OODA loop by observing the environment, orienting itself to prioritize valuable and/or vulnerable targets, decide on an action, and act autonomously. Speed increase: Having multiple parallel agents working towards a goal is a large shift compared to single operator or multiple operator augmented by AI. Scale: A single operator can target multiple organizations at the same time, greatly increasing their blast radius. Small mistakes are easily discovered: Autonomous frameworks relentlessly and systematically test exposed services, including their configurations. Architecture Planning model Built-in capabilities/execution environment Post-exploitation capabilities ARTEX (and forks) Planner and parallel agents Graph of goals, leads, and findings is linked to separate asset graph of target Directly on host or container with network/root access, can install/develop tools as needed Nothing built-in, requires user instruction LuaN1aoAgent Supervisor agent, planner agent, and generic executor agents Three graphs, with goals/tasks/blockers, evidence/hypothesises/exploits, and target/local Container with network/user access, can develop tools as needed and install user packages Built-in SSH and Chisel for tunneling and attempted reconnection after disruption Decepticon Orchestrator agent dispatching specialist sub-agents Graph of objectives with prerequisites Kali container running as root, can develop tools as needed Dedicated post-access, Active Directory and cloud pivoting skills Cairn Dispatcher orchestrating work to existing AI harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Pi) Graph of facts and leads; new nodes trigger dispatcher Kali container with root access or directly on host, can develop tools as needed Prompt guidance and Kali tools PentestGPT-Agent Supervisor agent and one generic executor agent Task list with dependencies, goals, and evidence Run on host, can develop tools as needed Nothing built-in, requires user instruction Observations from the world's largest network As of November 12, ARTEX and its forks make up over 60% of currently known AI penetration testing orchestrators. The charts below help us understand how adoption of these tools has changed over the past six weeks. Since the removal of the original ARTEX repository on October 8, traffic has grown more than tenfold, and has increased more than 30x since October 1. As demonstrated above, the takedown of ARTEX on October 8 (and widespread reporting of it) likely caused a hydra effect, where the removal of the original repository led to a massive increase in the number of forks and modifications which can be seen in the steep acceleration of unique instances around October 8. Identity-chained LLM exploitation Over the last eight weeks, our Cloudforce One team has been called into multiple incident response investigations involving ARTEX and ARTEX-derived LLM exploitation frameworks. We’ve seen firsthand how exposed credentials are being chained with LLM-based exploitation frameworks to gain the upper hand over defenders. We observed multiple incidents in which a threat actor gained initial access to a hyperscaler environment and pivoted directly into the customer's Cloudflare environment. Root-cause analysis revealed a common credential hygiene failure.

articles.content: We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability. The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery. As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity. That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range. We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm. We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%. Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow. The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery. The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features. October 05 19:11 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 38 minutes) Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes. Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features. What went wrong and why? Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted. Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs. How did we respond? A partial networking failure began, and actions jobs started backing up. Alerts flagged errors and slow job assignment, and we declared an incident. We redeployed the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners, but it did not recover. We traced the failures to the networking issue. We failed over the affected databases and storage to healthy regions, one service at a time, and added capacity. Actions recovered, but some other affected services kept failing even after failover. We worked with our cloud provider to resolve the networking failure. The remaining services recovered, and we resolved the incident. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We are making the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners better able to handle sudden increases in load, so it keeps up when another region shifts extra jobs to it. We now have expanded prioritization of runner assignment based on customer profile when available runner capacity is degraded. We are changing the behavior of GitHub-hosted runners to reduce recovery time when job assignment services are degraded for a period of time. We are improving how quickly we detect and locate partial network failures between our datacenters and the cloud-hosted services they depend on. October 06 19:57 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 43 minutes) Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused. Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request. Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed. What went wrong and why? A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database.

articles.content: Hey everyone! I've been experimenting a lot with AI coding agents like Claude Code and Codex, and one problem I kept running into was how difficult it is to coordinate agents when multiple developers are working on the same project. Most agent tools are designed around a single developer. But when you're working in a team, things get complicated pretty quickly: Agents can modify files another developer is responsible for. Multiple agents can end up working on the same task. Frontend and backend agents can make conflicting assumptions about API contracts. Coordinating everything manually through Slack, tickets, or copy-pasted prompts gets tedious. So I started building CodeRelay, an open-source tool built on top of T3 Code that focuses on collaboration between developers' coding agents. The idea is pretty simple: each developer owns certain parts of a repository, and when an agent needs something outside its owner's scope, it can hand off that work to the appropriate teammate's agent. How it works: Developers join a shared Team Hub and declare which parts of the repository they own. An agent can propose a task to another developer, including an API contract pinned to a specific Git commit. The receiving developer reviews and accepts the task into their own agent thread. Once the work is completed, the original developer gets the branch, commit, and summary to integrate. The goal isn't to replace existing coding agents, but to make them work better together across a team while keeping developers in control. There's also a local Alice/Bob demo you can run to test the entire handoff workflow without setting up a separate team. The project is still early, and I'd genuinely appreciate feedback, especially from developers already using multiple coding agents in shared repositories. GitHub: https://github.com/AymanAhsan/CodeRelay Website: https://site-olive-two-79.vercel.app/ I'm particularly curious: How are you currently coordinating AI coding agents across your team? Are you using worktrees, separate branches, manual handoffs, or something else?

articles.content: Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever. Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling. You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects. Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway. How it works You can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI , or REST API . In the dashboard , head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending. When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds. If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds or your spending limit. When the limit is reached, a blocking policy is enforced and your product is paused automatically. If you go to the dashboard , you can see the current billing cycle costs for each supported product in near real time (under 10 minutes), and manage your settings and thresholds from there. The overview panel tells you which products have thresholds and limits configured. In this example, you can see that Workers triggered two alerts before hitting the hard limit. Note that the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, not when you deploy a Worker or create a spending cap; a subscription starting October 10 generally has a cycle of October 10-November 10 — not a calendar month. The dashboard also shows an audit log, so you can see who changed a limit and when, or when a cap was reached. As with most Cloudflare services, Spend Management is also an API that you can use programmatically; the documentation can be found in our Developer Documentation . Here’s an example, but using the API: curl --fail-with-body --request POST \ "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID}/billing/spend-policies" \ --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \ --header "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }' And, of course, you can use cf, the CLI for the entire Cloudflare API : cf billing spend-policies list cf billing spend-policies create cf billing spend-policies get cf billing spend-policies update cf billing spend-policies delete cf billing spend-policies audit list cf billing spend-policies activity list cf billing spend-policies create --body '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }' Once a cap is enforced, new invocations of that product are rejected. Note that we only pause customer-code invocations that incur costs — in Workers, for example, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations are paused, but static assets continue to be served. To resume service, you can: Raise the limit above the current cycle’s accumulated spend. Disable or delete the blocking policy. Wait until the next billing cycle, when the existing block expires. That’s it. You can start using Spend Management for Workers and Durable Objects today, and other products will follow soon. Read on to learn how we built the system, and what’s going to happen next. How we built Spend Management As easy and straightforward as it seems on the surface, building a system like this at Cloudflare scale was no small feat. From an invocation anywhere on our distributed network to a blocking decision that we need to apply globally, building Spend Management required working with multiple teams, changing code in existing systems, and creating new systems from scratch. Let’s start by looking at the bird's-eye view of a capped billable event: Now let's dig deeper. Collecting and aggregating close to the source Each invocation produces usage measurements: requests, CPU time, execution duration, or storage operations, depending on the product. But transporting and processing this volume of raw data all the way from the sources down to the rating engine would not scale or be efficient. So what we do is we collect and aggregate the measurements as close to the source as possible using a two-stage metering pipeline that combines events into usage aggregates, so the engine sees accumulated usage rather than having to process all the events one by one. Let's look at a diagram. The first stage reduces raw-event volume close to parsing down to one-minute windows. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements, then combines matching measurements into typically one-minute buckets. Still, several records can describe the same account and time window. In the second stage, a separate service merges those first-stage partial aggregates using the same grouping rules, but over typically five-minute windows, and further reduces the volume before downstream processing by the Usage Engine. Here we also archive the consolidated aggregates; this gives us a durable dataset for later analytics and reconciliation. The nice thing about this two-stage pipeline is that it reduces the raw event volume early, so the downstream engines process only the aggregated usage they need to calculate spend and act on it. That’s what makes this practical at Cloudflare’s scale. Usage Engine: account-partitioned processing The Usage Engine translates aggregated measurements into usage records, which are standardized records containing the account, usage window, metric, quantity, and relevant dimensions. In other words, it maps product-specific meters into supported usage metrics. We partition processing by account, so an account’s usage and subscription information meet in the same place.

articles.content: When I return to a business owner for a second interview, the hardest task can be finding the first conversation. The recording exists, but its filename says almost nothing. The transcript lives elsewhere. A question I promised to revisit is buried in a notebook. An index can make that next conversation easier without turning reporting into database administration. I would start with one CSV file and a folder of recordings. Each interview gets a stable reference such as interview-001. That reference appears in the audio filename, transcript filename, and index row. A name can change; the reference should not. Keeping the identifier separate also makes it easier to share an outline without exposing a contributor’s contact details. What belongs in the row? I use a compact structure: reference, recording date, business type, relative audio path, transcript path, follow-up topic, and next review date. Permission status deserves its own field. Empty means unknown, not yes. Sensitive contact information belongs in a separate protected address book rather than a spreadsheet that might travel with a draft or get attached to an email. The first useful script is a checker. It reads the CSV, joins each relative path to the project folder, and reports files that are missing. It also flags duplicate references and dates that cannot be parsed. Those checks catch mistakes early. They do not decide what an interview means. The writer still needs to listen, read, and make the editorial choices. A second script can produce a simple follow-up list. Compare each review date with today, then print the overdue rows and their open questions. Keep the output local and short. I want to see that an owner planned to train an assistant, not receive an automatic message claiming the training happened. Reminders are useful precisely because they send me back to the source. Search can stay plain. A small HTML page can load a prepared JSON export and filter records by topic or business type. Render interview notes as text rather than inserting them as HTML. Keep the export free of phone numbers, private addresses, and unapproved quotations. Before sharing anything, check the actual exported file. Hiding a column on screen does not remove its underlying data. Backups need a little care. Copy the project folder to another drive, verify that a sample recording opens, and keep versions of the index. A successful copy message is not the same as a successful recovery. Relative paths help here: moving the whole project should preserve its internal references. Test that assumption on a copy before relying on it during a deadline. Would I build a bigger application? Only after the small version reveals a real need. A useful reporting tool should reduce the effort of finding evidence, not create another inbox to maintain. Start with ten interviews, run the checks, and note what remains awkward. The reward is modest but worthwhile: less time hunting for a recording, and more attention available for the person whose business I am trying to understand.
