articles.content: How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline. An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database. I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” . Define one job and when it applies A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent , we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose: --- name: proof-agent description: Adversarial verification of AI-generated work. Spawns an independent verifier to check for false claims, broken code, and security issues. --- At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification. The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings. Coordinate multiple skills for a larger workflow When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together. In the support-desk pipeline example , we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need. The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests. Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone. Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit. Keep project configuration out of the skill We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions: project: name: "support-desk" store_name: "support_metric_store" platform: engine: "duckdb" pipeline_framework: "spark_python" duckdb_dir: "warehouse" With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project. Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them? Share execution paths between skills The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic. The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access. Put checks and approval points in the workflow The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval. The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS , FAIL , or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules. Package for each agent client, then verify its setup Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync.

articles.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
articles.headline: GitHub introduces agent skills for reusable AI workflows
articles.summary: GitHub Blog announces agent skills, versioned directories centered on SKILL.md files that capture repeatable instructions for AI agents. The feature allows teams to define tasks with clear inputs and outputs, coordinate multiple skills in workflows like Data Forge, and share execution paths via a manifest. Skills can describe tasks such as database queries or code verification, though the environment must still provide necessary tools and permissions. The approach aims to reduce context loss and institutional knowledge silos by enabling reusable, portable workflows across different agents and projects.

articles.content: Getting a docs site into a vector database once is the easy part. Keeping it current is where most RAG projects quietly fail: the docs change every week, the index doesn't, and the assistant keeps citing a page that was rewritten a month ago. A nightly full re-crawl fixes freshness but re-embeds thousands of unchanged chunks to pick up a handful of edits, and still leaves deleted pages in the index. What a sync actually needs is a list of operations: these chunks are new or edited, upsert them; these chunk IDs no longer exist, delete them. This post gets that list from a scheduled run, one row per chunk, and applies it to Pinecone or Qdrant, or lets the run write it there itself. Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built Website to Knowledge Base Sync . It's a paid tool (prices below). What a run returns You give it public start URLs (or a sitemap). The first run returns every chunk of the site's main content as op: "upsert" . Every later run with the same input re-checks the site and returns only: op: "upsert" rows for chunks that are new or whose text changed, with text , heading_path , citation and chunk_url (the page URL with the heading's #anchor ); op: "delete" rows for chunk IDs that are gone, with a reason such as chunk changed or removed or page returned HTTP 404 . A page with no edits returns nothing. A run with no edits returns an empty dataset and a summary of what it checked. The part that makes this work is the ID. chunk_id is a UUID made from the page URL, the heading path and a hash of the chunk's normalized text, and chunk boundaries are cut at content-defined points rather than fixed offsets. Editing one paragraph changes the ID of the chunk it sits in (rarely also the next one); every other chunk on the page keeps its ID, so you never re-embed it. Menus, footers, cookie banners and "Last updated" lines are stripped before chunking, so layout changes are not changes. A page that errors, shows a bot challenge, comes back as an empty JavaScript shell or suddenly shrinks by more than 90% keeps its chunks: it is listed in the run summary and never turned into deletes. Only a 404/410 or a redirect away deletes a page's chunks. Option 1: apply the rows yourself This uses Qdrant's Python client and OpenAI embeddings; the same loop works with any store that takes UUID IDs. pip install apify-client qdrant-client openai import os from apify_client import ApifyClient from openai import OpenAI from qdrant_client import QdrantClient , models apify = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ "APIFY_TOKEN" ] ) run = apify . actor ( "aurelix/rag-site-sync" ) . call ( run_input = { "startUrls" : [ "https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/" ] , "syncId" : "python-tutorial" , "maxPages" : 100 , } ) rows = list ( apify . dataset ( run [ "defaultDatasetId" ] ) . iterate_items ( ) ) upserts = [ r for r in rows if r [ "op" ] == "upsert" ] deletes = [ r [ "chunk_id" ] for r in rows if r [ "op" ] == "delete" ] qdrant = QdrantClient ( url = os . environ [ "QDRANT_URL" ] , api_key = os . environ [ "QDRANT_API_KEY" ] ) if not qdrant . collection_exists ( "docs" ) : qdrant . create_collection ( "docs" , vectors_config = models . VectorParams ( size = 1536 , distance = models . Distance . COSINE ) ) if deletes : qdrant . delete ( "docs" , points_selector = models . PointIdsList ( points = deletes ) ) oai = OpenAI ( ) for i in range ( 0 , len ( upserts ) , 100 ) : batch = upserts [ i : i + 100 ] vectors = oai . embeddings . create ( model = "text-embedding-3-small" , input = [ r [ "text" ] for r in batch ] ) . data qdrant . upsert ( "docs" , points = [ models . PointStruct ( id = r [ "chunk_id" ] , vector = v . embedding , payload = { "text" : r [ "text" ] , "url" : r [ "chunk_url" ] , "citation" : r [ "citation" ] } ) for r , v in zip ( batch , vectors ) ] ) print ( f "{len(upserts)} chunks upserted, {len(deletes)} deleted" ) Run it once to fill the collection, then on a schedule. On a quiet day rows is empty and nothing is embedded. Option 2: let the run write to your index If you would rather not run any code, give the Actor your own keys and it applies each page's deletes and upserts before moving on: { "startUrls" : [ "https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/" ] , "syncId" : "python-tutorial" , "maxPages" : 100 , "vectorDatabase" : "pinecone" , "pineconeApiKey" : "<your Pinecone key>" , "pineconeIndexHost" : "<your index host>" , "pineconeNamespace" : "python-docs" , "openaiApiKey" : "<your OpenAI key>" } Pinecone : with an OpenAI key, chunks are embedded and written as vectors with text , url , citation and heading_path as metadata. Without one, the run uses your index's integrated embedding and writes text records (set pineconeTextField to the field your index embeds). Qdrant : qdrantUrl , qdrantApiKey , qdrantCollection and an OpenAI key; the collection is created with cosine distance if it does not exist. Keys are secret inputs, checked before any page is fetched; a wrong key ends the run at once with only the start fee. If the database refuses a write mid-run, the run stops, that page is not charged and it is sent again next run, so the index never silently misses a change. Embedding is done only for new and edited chunks, on your own OpenAI account. Save the input as a task in the Apify Console and click Schedule for a daily sync.

articles.content: For a while now I have been working on Lonca, a version control system for AI agents. This post starts a series about it. Later posts will take its parts one at a time; this first one only gives the overall picture: what Lonca is, which problem it tries to solve, and how much of that it does today, in version 0.2.3. I will try not to oversell it. I will write down what works, and also what does not exist yet. Lonca in short: version control for AI agents Lonca is a version control system for repositories where several AI agents and a few humans work at the same time. It is written in Rust and it is open source (Apache-2.0). It does not try to replace Git. The content stays plain Git: you can push to GitHub, and your Git tools keep working. What changes is everything around it: who may do what, how work done at the same time is merged, and how every operation is recorded and checked. The name comes from the craft guilds of the Ottoman bazaar, the lonca : written rules, masters, journeymen and apprentices, and an inspection before goods reach the market. That is Lonca's model too. The problem it solves Most days I run several coding agents on the same repository. The agents do their work well; the problem is the tooling around them. Git and platforms like GitHub assume that every writer is a person. With agents, that assumption breaks in three places: Permissions. An agent works with my token, shows up in the history under my name, and has every right I have. Even when its task is to fix one function, it can force-push, delete a branch or change the CI files. Nothing stands in between. Concurrency. Two agents working on the same file only find out about each other at merge time. Each is green on its own; together they are red. Accountability. When something goes wrong, I can't answer the two questions that matter: what was this agent allowed to do, and did it do only that? Lonca exists to answer these three. How it works The core idea is simple: agents never write to the repository directly, they propose . A single process on the machine, the Lonca daemon, is the repository's only writer. It decides every request, signs the decision, appends it to an operation log kept inside the repository ( refs/lonca/oplog ), and only then applies it. Agents propose; the daemon, the only writer, decides, signs and records. Four parts around the daemon Four parts are built around that: Capabilities, not accounts. Every agent works in a session, and the session gets narrow rights that expire: which paths it may touch, which operations it may run, size limits. Rights can only narrow when they are handed to sub-agents. Revoking a session revokes everything derived from it. Unknown operations, scopes and paths are refused. Symbol leases and a structural merge queue. Agents lease the functions and types they edit, so several agents can work in parallel on different functions of the same file. When an agent proposes a change, it declares what it changed; Lonca computes what really changed with tree-sitter and refuses the proposal if the two don't match. The merge queue merges changes symbol by symbol and runs the build and tests in a sandbox with no network access; trunk moves only after that. Taint. The tool the agent runs in (the harness; today that is Claude Code) reports every tool call to the daemon, and a proxy sees outbound connections. A session that reads outside content (a web page, an issue, another MCP server) counts as tainted: its changes need a human's approval, and it may not touch build scripts, CI or lock files at all. This is the structural answer to prompt injection. A log anyone can replay. Every operation, whether allowed, denied or sent to a human, is in the log, and the log travels with the repository on git push . The log is append-only; an undo ( lonca undo ) is a new, compensating operation. The independent auditor, lonca-audit , replays every decision from the start, recomputes every merge, and catches a forged entry even when it is signed with the daemon's own key. Human signatures, and no AI where integrity depends on it Humans sign their own operations with their own keys. The key can live in the Mac's Secure Enclave or on a FIDO security key; then every approval needs Touch ID or a touch. An agent running as your user can't approve on your behalf. There is no AI where integrity depends on it. The decision function decide() , the daemon and the auditor contain no AI, no network and no randomness. decide() is a pure function, and all of its inputs, time included, are in the log entry. Build and test results are recorded as evidence and never recomputed later. AI appears only as an optional advisor that helps a human during review, and it decides nothing. Where it stands today The current version is 0.2.3. Every phase of the design is implemented and tested. A log written by any 0.x release stays readable and auditable by every later release. What it does today Full support for Claude Code. I build Lonca against Claude Code and try it live before every release. The hooks and Lonca's MCP tools are ready as soon as a session starts. Symbol-level work in 13 languages. Rust, Python, TypeScript/TSX, JavaScript, C#, Go, Java, Kotlin, C, C++, Ruby, PHP and Swift. Markdown, TOML, JSON and YAML files are split into sections; other files are leased whole. macOS and Linux. Installed with Homebrew, install.sh or cargo install . Tests. More than 1,800 tests, real sandbox and socket tests included. 45 acceptance criteria, run with the real binaries and real daemon processes, must pass before every release. Eight fuzz targets must also be green before every release.

articles.headline: Lonca 0.2.3: version control system for AI coding agents
articles.summary: Lonca 0.2.3 is an open-source version control system for AI agents working on repositories, written in Rust. It operates alongside Git, managing agent permissions, concurrency, and accountability through a daemon that mediates all changes. Key features include symbolic leases for parallel editing, a structural merge queue, and taint detection for prompt injection prevention. All operations are logged and auditable, with human signatures required for critical actions. It currently supports Claude Code and 13 programming languages across macOS and Linux.

articles.content: Quick answer: Use a resource template when the model needs parameterized, read-only access to data that has an address, such as a file path or a record id, and use a tool when the call performs an action, may have side effects, or needs approval. A resource template is a fill-in URI the host reads from; a tool is a named function the model invokes. When a read could be modeled either way, default to a resource for addressable data and a tool for anything that writes or computes. What each primitive is Resources are the readable data a server exposes. Each resource has a URI, a name, and an optional MIME type, and the client fetches it with a resources/read call. Tools are functions the model can call: each has a name, description, and input schema, and a tools/call runs it and returns structured content. Resources sit on the read side of that line, while tools cover the operations. Resource templates in one minute A plain resource is one fixed URI. A resource template is a parameterized URI following the URI template pattern, such as file:///{path} or https://api.example.com/users/{id} , that the server advertises so the client can fill in the braces and construct a valid address. The model supplies the parameter, the host builds the URI, and the same read path handles every value. This keeps the data addressable: a fetched result points to a real URI that can be referenced, re-read, or cached rather than existing only as the output of a function. Side-by-side Dimension Resource template Tool Intent Read data Do work or compute Input Parameters in a URI Structured schema arguments Side effects None expected Possible, often approved Addressability Each result has a URI Result is not inherently addressable Caching Reads can be cached Usually not cached Host control Treated as data access Often gated by user consent Where they overlap A read by id is the case where both work. users/{id} as a resource template says "this record lives at this address." A get_user tool says "call this function with an id and take the result." The semantics differ even when the bytes come back identical. Prefer the template when the same data is read repeatedly, linked from elsewhere, or shown in a browser of available data. Prefer the tool when the read is really the start of a workflow, applies logic beyond a simple fetch, or must sit alongside write operations the model already calls. How the model actually reaches them Tools are the path models are most reliable at invoking automatically, because tool selection is built into the model's call loop. Resource discovery and automatic reads vary more across hosts; some surface resources through an attachment or picker rather than letting the model fire reads on its own. If a value must be fetched autonomously every time, a tool is often the safer bet. If the goal is addressable, user-browsable data that the host can list and read, resources fit better. To confirm what a server actually returns for either primitive, send the calls and inspect the responses in a local workspace; Powerduck keeps those reads visible so the choice is based on observed behavior. Honest limits The protocol defines the shapes, not a hard rule that every read must be a resource, and hosts differ in how they expose resources to the model. A resource being read-only is a convention the server is expected to honor; the protocol does not prove the handler never mutates state. A template also does not validate that the underlying data is current or correct. Connecting a server does not deploy a backend, and these primitives do not replace the real system the data comes from. Frequently asked questions Is a resource template just a read-only tool? It is read-only and addressable, but the model reaches it through a constructed URI rather than a function call, and the host treats it as data rather than an action. Can a parameterized read be a tool instead? Yes. Use a tool when the read involves logic, starts a workflow, or needs the same consent path as write operations. Do models call resources automatically? Support varies by host; tools are the more consistent path for autonomous invocation, while resources are often surfaced through browsing or attachment UI. Can a resource template have side effects? It is meant to be read-only, so a handler that mutates state breaks the expected contract. The bottom line Choose by intent: addressable, parameterized reads belong in resource templates, and actions that compute or change state belong in tools. If the result has a URI that should be linked or cached, lean resource; if the model must reliably trigger it or it needs approval, lean tool. For more on building these servers, see the MCP server guide hub .

articles.content: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks . When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally. A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory. Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array. This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected. The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied. Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git. Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute. The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges. The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream. Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files. These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features . Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream. [ Advisory ] Additional hardening Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory. Protecting GitHub users We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible. We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git. GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git. Update Git Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users. If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes. Get an updated version of Git >

articles.content: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works. What we’re building and why it’s unique Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm. Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge. Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put . Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper. Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale . A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements . The challenges of consensus at a global scale While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable. Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers. Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues. Destructive interference and leaders Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits. Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal. Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance. When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony. To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast. The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place. When leader recovery is unstable When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.
articles.excerpt: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication.
articles.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
articles.headline: Cloudflare announces Meerkat, experimental distributed consensus service powered by QuePaxa algorithm
articles.summary: Cloudflare announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage its internal global control plane. Powered by the new QuePaxa consensus algorithm, Meerkat addresses limitations of traditional leader-based systems like Raft and Paxos, which degrade under wide-area network volatility. Unlike established algorithms relying on a single leader, QuePaxa promises better stability by avoiding destructive interference and inaccurate fault detection. The system ensures replicas maintain consistent logs despite high latency and broken connections, preventing the unavailability and performance degradation seen in previous Cloudflare incidents.

articles.content: Email test fixtures are often treated as harmless plumbing. A test creates an address, waits for a verification message, clicks a link, and deletes the data. In practice, that fixture can contain a name, a token, a password-reset URL, or a copy of product behavior that was never meant to leave a staging system. The useful question is not whether a test inbox is temporary. It is whether the team understands what can happen to the data before, during, and after the test. A short-lived inbox can still be copied into logs or reused by a parallel run. This is the same kind of boundary I look for when reviewing a web workflow: make the ownership and failure states visible, then choose tools that fit the risk. Teams sometimes search for “temp mail so” or “use and throw email” when they need a quick fixture, but the search phrase should not become the security design. Why email fixtures deserve a threat model An email fixture crosses several trust boundaries: the test runner creates an identity; the application stores or sends a message; a mailbox provider receives and retains content; the test reads a token and may print it in a failure report; cleanup attempts to remove the data after the run. Each boundary has a different owner. If the fixture are managed as one simple variable, nobody may be responsible for retention, access, or cleanup. The threat model does not need to be a large document. A one-page map is enough to identify sensitive content, allowed readers, expected lifetime, and what happens when cleanup fails. Map the data before choosing the inbox Start with the message, not the provider. List the fields a test can observe: Recipient address and any identifying label. Verification or reset token. Subject and body, including links and feature flags. Timestamps, message IDs, and correlation IDs. Screenshots, traces, and CI logs created when an assertion fails. Then mark where each field can be copied. A token may move from the message to the browser URL, then into a trace archive. An address may appear in a test name and remain in a dashboard for weeks. The original inbox might expire correctly while the secondary copies doesnt. This inventory also explains why “temporary” is not the same as “private”. Deletion at the source is useful, but it does not remove every derived artefact. Keep these informations in the test design review, not only in a provider configuration file. For event-driven systems, a small failure lab for replayable webhooks is a helpful companion idea: make retries and duplicate delivery observable instead of assuming the first attempt is the only attempt. Four questions for a useful threat model Who can read the fixture? The answer should include CI workers, test developers, support tools, and the mailbox API. If a shared dashboard can show message bodies, treat it as an email reader. Least privilege applies here too: a test that only needs a verification link should not receive every message in a shared inbox. What is the maximum lifetime? Choose a deadline for the address, the message, and copied artifacts. The deadlines may differ, but they should be explicit. A cleanup check should report a failed delete. What can be replayed? Verification links and reset tokens are credentials for a short period. They should be scoped to the test run, invalidated after use, and excluded from long-lived logs. If a failure report contains a live token, redact it before storing the report. What happens when isolation fails? Parallel tests need unique identities and a way to prove that a message belongs to the current run. A useful correlation value can be put in a test-only header or subject, while the assertion still checks the recipient and token. “It usually finds the right email” is not an isolation guarantee. Turn the model into engineering controls The threat model matters only when it changes the implementation. I usually expect these controls: Run-scoped identities: derive an address or mailbox key from a run ID, never from a hard-coded shared account. Narrow API permissions: separate message creation, reading, and deletion where the provider allows it. Redacted observability: log IDs and states, not full bodies or credential-bearing URLs. Bounded polling: stop waiting at a known deadline and classify the result as received, expired, or rejected. Explicit cleanup: run cleanup in a deferred step and emit an alert when it fails. Retention tests: periodically verify that old fixtures and their traces are actually gone. The same controls help whether the inbox is local, hosted, or a simple “tempail mail” search result. Product names change; ownership and retention questions remain. Also, “tempail” is an easy typo to carry into documentation, so keep operational terms and provider names reviewed seperately. For authentication flows, a state ledger for OAuth callback tests shows the broader principle: a test should be able to explain which state it created and which callback consumed it. A practical review checklist Before approving an email fixture, ask: Is the message content synthetic and non-sensitive? Is each mailbox identity unique to a run or a bounded test group? Are tokens redacted from logs, screenshots, and traces? Is there a documented expiration and a measured cleanup result? Can a parallel test prove that it owns the message it found? Does a provider outage fail clearly instead of causing indefinite retries? This checklist catches accidental exposure and gives maintainers a shared vocabulary when a test grows beyond its original purpose. Q&A Should every email test use a disposable inbox? No. Unit tests should usually mock the mail boundary. Integration tests can use a local capture service. End-to-end tests may need a controlled external inbox when delivery itself is part of the behavior. Choose the smallest environment that proves the claim. Is deleting the inbox enough? Not always. Check logs, traces, screenshots, provider retention, and backups that are inside your control. The goal is not perfect certainty; it is a stated retention policy with checks that reveal drift.

articles.content: A high severity score can look inconsistent with an advisory that describes several conditions and no known exploitation. CVE-2026-114125 is a useful example of why the two statements can both be true. CVSS measures the potential impact and exploitability of a vulnerability under its stated metrics. Exploitation observations answer a different question. What the CVSS v4 score says The GitHub Reviewed advisory assigns 9.4 Critical using CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:H/SI:H/SA:H . The attack vector is Network, attack complexity is Low, attack requirements are None, and no privileges are required. Passive user interaction is present. The vulnerable system and subsequent system impacts are high for confidentiality, integrity, and availability. That vector reflects a potentially serious outcome. A malicious website can provide the network-facing content while the developer's browser supplies access to a local Storybook server. No prior account on the target is required. If the chain succeeds, the developer's project and permissions become the relevant boundary. The advisory also says the attack relies on correctly exploiting a sequence of many vulnerabilities, some of which were not disclosed to the Storybook team. That wording limits what can be inferred from the score. CVSS is not a claim that the published advisory contains a simple one-request exploit. Likelihood has separate evidence The GitHub advisory lists an EPSS score of 0.385 percent, in the 33rd percentile. Storybook says it is not aware of exploitation in the wild. Those signals suggest a lower observed or predicted urgency than the critical rating alone might imply. They do not establish that no attacker will use the chain, and EPSS is a time-bounded estimate rather than a verdict on one organization's exposure. Risk assessment should combine the score with local conditions. A vulnerable dev server that a person opens while browsing untrusted sites is materially different from a server that is not installed or never runs. A workstation with production credentials and broad network access has a different blast radius from an isolated test environment. Why file modification matters The advisory's worst case starts with unauthorized changes to story files. Story files are inputs to development and testing workflows, not inert documentation. They may be imported by a test runner, browser runtime, or local tool. If the attacker can shape those files and cause a later process to execute them, the impact expands from repository integrity to code execution. Several outcomes deserve separate treatment: A malicious site reaches the preview but no file changes are observed. Story files change, but no execution path consumes the modification. Changed files enter a local process with the developer's privileges. The process can access credentials, source, or internal systems beyond the repository. Only the stronger outcomes justify claims of code execution or credential compromise. The lower outcomes still require investigation and remediation because they show that the trust boundary failed. The vulnerable population is not one number The affected package ranges cover Storybook 8, 9, 10, and 11 alpha releases. Built output is not affected, and dev servers that are never opened in a browser fall outside the published path. A ZoomEye search for title="Storybook" produced 5,438 matches, while the CVE-specific filter produced zero. The title count is a product fingerprint, not a vulnerable-version census, and it cannot measure private developer laptops. Organizations should score exposure at the asset level. Inputs include installed version, interactive browser use, bind address, browser localhost permissions, feature flags, and the privileges of local test and build processes. This produces a more useful likelihood estimate than applying 9.4 uniformly to every Storybook title. Turning the model into action Patch to 8.6.19, 9.1.21, 10.6.2, or 11.0.0-alpha.6. Stop affected interactive servers until the update is in place. Remove insecure iframe and messaging flags unless a reviewed compatibility requirement remains. Keep development servers on loopback where possible and preserve host validation when LAN sharing is necessary. The patched defaults are part of risk reduction. They block cross-host development iframe embedding and reject unknown message origins. Update Chromatic's Visual Tests addon to 5.5.1 or later where needed. Then verify the runtime, not just the package declaration. A conditional exploit can still justify a critical score when successful execution reaches developer permissions. The practical response is to reduce the number of environments that meet those conditions and to preserve evidence when the chain may have progressed. References GitHub Advisory Database: CVE-2026-114125 Storybook v10.6.2 release Storybook security patch pull request SecurityOnline vulnerability report

articles.content: Qwen Image 2.1 is the newest image model from Alibaba's Qwen team, and it is the one I open on PixelDojo when the picture has to carry real type: a poster title, a date line, a label, or small print that needs to be spelled right. It renders natively at 2K. This is not an upscale. A 3:4 portrait comes back at 1792 by 2400, with the lines, silver hair, and wool fibers still intact. It can also edit or combine up to 10 reference images, and it can run up to 3 LoRAs you train yourself. There is a longer Qwen Image 2.1 prompting guide with the copy-ready prompts and the images each one made. The Qwen Image 2.1 tool page is where you actually run them. This post is the shorter version of how I write for it. A short from All Your Tech built from Qwen Image 2.1 stills: one truck, a sinkhole, seven shots. Qwen Turbo for drafts, the full model for finals Qwen Image 2.1 comes in two versions, and they share the same strengths. Qwen Image 2.1 Turbo is the everyday pick. It makes an image in 8 steps. A 2K image is 0.5 credits. It is a good fit for posters, product shots, food, interiors, and LoRA tests. The full Qwen Image 2.1 takes 40 steps and is the one to switch to for final art, very small print, or a negative prompt when you need one. A 2K image is 1.5 credits. On every plan, Qwen Image 2.1 is also unlimited in Relax mode at 1K, with no credits spent. A practical loop from the guide: shape the idea on Turbo at 1K for 0.25 credits, then render the final on the full model at 2K for 1.5 credits. A new model or a new size is a new image, so judge the final on its own, not as a straight enlarge of the draft. The five-part Qwen prompt from the guide Qwen works better when the prompt names the piece first and the details second. The piece. "Typographic concert poster." "Editorial portrait, medium close-up." "Product hero shot." The subject. Specific enough to picture: a woman in her sixties with a silver bob and round tortoiseshell glasses, or a frosted glass perfume bottle with a brass cap. The setting and action. Where it is, and what is happening. The light and the finish. A lens, a kind of grain, a palette, where the sun falls. The type, if any. Every word that should appear goes in double quotes, with a place for it: across the top, small at the bottom, on the label. Name the type style too. Bold condensed, classic serif, hand lettered, clean sans serif. If you leave that out, you are rolling the dice on the lettering. A Qwen poster prompt you can copy This is the concert poster from the guide, run on Turbo at 2K for 0.5 credits: Typographic concert poster, bold condensed letters "SALT AND STATIC" stacked across the top, a lone saxophonist silhouetted against a huge coral moon over a quiet harbor, screen-print grain, deep navy and coral palette, small text at the bottom reading "AUGUST 14 TO 16, PIER 9" The SALT AND STATIC poster from the guide, run on Turbo at 2K. The useful bits are all in one sentence: the kind of piece, the type style, the quoted title and where it sits, one image in the middle, a two-color palette, and a quoted date line at the bottom. The same shape works for a product shot. Product, surface, one prop, one tactile detail (droplets on the glass), then the light and the backdrop color. Swap in your own bottle and keep the rest of the sentence. A product hero from the guide, the same prompt shape as the poster, swapped to a bottle. For an overhead food photo, list every dish after a colon. Each one tends to land on the tray. "Steam rising" and "soft window light from the left" are enough to set the mood without a paragraph of food styling language. Qwen reference images and LoRAs Leave the reference slot empty and it is a text-to-image model. Attach one to ten images and the prompt becomes an instruction: change this, keep that, put the product from image 1 into the scene from image 2. Give each reference a number and a job, and for edits list the change and then list what must stay (the face, the label, the camera angle). You can train a LoRA on PixelDojo and then call it from Qwen Image 2.1, stacking up to 3 in one image. In the guide we trained one on 8 photos of a ceramic owl, then used a one-line prompt: a photo of zzqwowl sitting on a stack of pancakes in a retro diner, warm morning light The ceramic owl LoRA from the guide, called with a one-line prompt and the zzqwowl trigger. The trigger word stands in for the subject. The prompt never had to mention the glaze or the eye color, because the LoRA already carries them. Use a made-up trigger (like zzqwowl) so it does not collide with a real word. Strength 1 is the default. Turn it down a little when you stack a subject LoRA with a style LoRA, so neither one takes over. When I pick Qwen Image I pick Qwen Image 2.1 when the type has to be right, when I want native 2K rather than an upscale, or when I want to drop a trained LoRA into a new scene. Turbo is how I would draft. The full model is how I would finish anything with a lot of small detail in one frame. If you want the rest of the prompts (the tram portrait, the perfume hero, the whale matte painting, the oak interior), they are in the Qwen Image prompting guide , each next to the image it made.

articles.summary: Alibaba's Qwen team released Qwen Image 2.1, an image model that renders native 2K resolution without upscaling. The model can edit or combine up to 10 reference images and run up to 3 custom LoRAs. It is available in Turbo and full versions, with Turbo generating images in 8 steps for 0.5 credits and the full model in 40 steps for 1.5 credits. Users can generate unlimited 1K images in Relax mode at no cost. The model excels at precise typography and detailed rendering for posters, product shots, and food photography.

articles.content: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem. When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start. Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent. AI is changing open source AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests. The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown. During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase. AI has raised the pressure to produce . It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals. Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment. One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e , a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says. Fund distribution The recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare. The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of: Contributions to ecosystem recipients Stipends to core maintainers We’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation. We'll continue to distribute and draw down the committed amount every quarter. Contributions to ecosystem recipients This first round of sponsorships prioritized dependencies, ecosystem critical plugins, significant contributors, and projects that moved the ecosystem forward. Andrew Gallant Andrey Sitnik Anthony Fu Fund Ari Perkkiö Artem Zakharchenko Babel Bart Waardenburg Benjamin E. Coe Brandon Roberts Chai David Ortner David Tolnay Denis Bardadym Devon Govett Divyansh Singh e18e ESlint Giorgio Boa Guy Bedford Jessica Sachs Jonas Kruckenberg Luigi Pinca Máximo Mussini Michael Cousins Mickael Jeanroy Misha Kaletsky Mock Service Worker Mohammad Bagher Abiyat Nicholas Rayburn Paul Miller Pig Fang pnpm Polka PostCSS Prettier Ralf Jung Rollup Sindre Sorhus Terser typescript-eslint Verite universal-deploy (Vike) Younes Jaaidi Yuki Okushi Stipends to core maintainers The core maintainers of the Vite stack are eligible for a stipend of up to $4,000 per calendar month. Each maintainer can invoice at a rate of $50 per hour contributed that month. Any time spent improving or supporting the project in some way counts towards this stipend: writing code, writing documentation, triaging issues, offering support in our Discord servers, attending meetings or meetups, contributing to our upstream dependencies, and so on. Maintainers who are already being paid for or employed for this work do not receive stipends — for example, VoidZero employees are ineligible. Cloudflare supports open source Cloudflare’s mission is to help build a better Internet. Supporting open source falls squarely within that mission. The Vite Ecosystem Fund is only part of it. Cloudflare committed an additional $1 million to sponsor open source projects in our Community Engineers Fund. We also provide Cloudflare credits to open source projects via Project Alexandria . The Vite ecosystem has come this far because of all the maintainers and contributors who came together to build a community. These sponsorships are a small thank-you for all this hard work.

articles.content: Short answer: among the 404 public Sylius plugins that are still active, 59.4% have a stable release compatible with Sylius 2. Weighted by monthly downloads, that rises to 83%, which still leaves 17% of installs on plugins that are not ready under their current name. Sylius 1.14 security support ends on December 31, 2026. A shop can only upgrade once every plugin it uses has a compatible release, so I classified every package of type sylius-plugin on Packagist (802 of them, data from November 14, 2026) from the version constraints of each release. The full report, the dataset and the scripts are on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24224419 Method in one paragraph Only constraints on packages that follow Sylius numbering count ( sylius/sylius and the 41 sub-packages it replaces). A release is compatible if its constraints accept at least one of the 53 stable Sylius 2 releases, if it was published after Sylius 2.0.0 (November 12, 2024), and if at least one constraint names Sylius 2 explicitly. That last rule matters: an open-ended >=1.9 accepts Sylius 2 by accident. My first version of the study missed it and counted three plugins as compatible when they are not; version 1.1 fixes it. Results Category All (782) Active (404) Share of monthly downloads Stable Sylius 2 release 247 (31.6%) 240 (59.4%) 83.0% Pre-release only 13 12 4.4% Development branch only 32 11 1.6% Replaced by another package 5 3 3.6% Deprecated, no successor 3 1 1.2% Sylius 1 only 482 (61.6%) 137 6.2% 338 of the "Sylius 1 only" plugins have had no release since 2024. They are not coming. Three things worth knowing Renamed packages. BitBag's CMS and Wishlist plugins moved to the Sylius organisation ( sylius/cms-plugin , sylius/wishlist-plugin ). The FLUX-SE Payum Stripe plugin points to the official Stripe plugin, and Mollie did the same. Upgrading means switching packages, not bumping a constraint. No successor. sylius/admin-order-creation-plugin (6,000+ downloads a month) is deprecated by the Sylius team with no open-source replacement. Adoption is accelerating. 65 plugins shipped their first Sylius 2 compatible release between October 1 and November 14, 2026, more than in any full quarter before. Check your own project Sylius Upgrade Analyzer (MIT, which I maintain) checks every plugin in your composer.json against the target version, along with the rest of the breaking changes. The Docker image runs whatever PHP version your project is on: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/project" ghcr.io/pierrearthurdemengel/sylius-upgrade-analyzer Disclosure: I do Sylius 1 to 2 migrations for a living. If you want a second pair of eyes on your upgrade: https://creation-site-pro.fr/en/sylius-2-upgrade?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=plugin-study

articles.headline: Sylius 2 compatibility found in 59.4% of active plugins, 83% by downloads
articles.summary: An analysis of 802 Sylius plugins from Packagist found that 59.4% of the 404 active plugins have a stable release compatible with Sylius 2. Weighted by monthly downloads, compatibility rises to 83%, leaving 17% of installs on unready plugins. Sylius 1.14 security support ends December 31, 2026. The study notes that 338 'Sylius 1 only' plugins have had no release since 2024, and 65 plugins released their first Sylius 2 compatible version between October and November 2026. It also warns that upgrading requires switching packages, not just bumping constraints, as some deprecated plugins have no successor.

articles.content: Everyone says "just start freelancing." Nobody says how you get the first client when you have no reviews, no portfolio full of paid work, and no idea what to charge. That's the catch-22: clients want experience, and you need clients to get experience. I'll be honest up front. Your first client rarely arrives from a magical platform or a viral post. It comes from a small, specific offer put in front of the right person. This guide walks through exactly how to do that, step by step, without pretending it's easy or promising numbers I can't back up. 1. A Quick Reality Check Before we get into tactics, let's set expectations: The first client is the hardest. The second is easier, the third easier still. It's slow at the start. Expect weeks, not days. Money will be small at first. The bigger prize is proof: a real project, a real testimonial, a real story. It's a skill of its own. Finding clients, scoping work, and communicating well matter as much as coding. None of this should discourage you. It should make you patient, which is the trait that separates people who land clients from people who give up after three cold messages. 2. Think of It as Fishing in the Right Pond Imagine fishing in the middle of the ocean with a huge net. You'll catch a lot of water and very little else. Now imagine picking one small pond where you know the fish are hungry, and using the right bait. Much better odds. Beginner freelancers usually do the ocean version: "I'm a developer, hire me!" posted everywhere, aimed at everyone. Nobody knows what to do with that. The winning move is the pond version: choose one type of client and one specific problem you solve for them. 3. Pick Your Pond (Your Niche) Look close to home, at people who need something simple built and don't know where to start: Local shops, cafés, salons, and restaurants without a website, or with an outdated one Coaching centers, tuition teachers, and training institutes Student clubs, college events, and societies Small event organizers, photographers, and freelancers who need a portfolio site Family-run businesses that still take orders by phone or chat Pick one group you understand. Knowing your audience makes your pitch sound sharper, because you can speak their language. 4. Make One Narrow, Clear Offer "Full-stack web developer" tells a shop owner nothing. Compare that with: "I build simple one-page websites for local restaurants, with menu, location, and a contact button." "I redesign outdated landing pages so they load fast and look good on phones." "I set up a small online booking form for salons and coaching centers." A narrow offer is easier to understand, easier to price, and easier to say yes to. You can always widen it once you have clients. Start with something you can deliver confidently in a couple of weeks. 5. Build Proof Before You Pitch You don't have paid work yet, so create the next best thing. Make two or three sample projects that match your offer. A demo restaurant site, a mock landing page for a coaching center, a booking form. Do a concept redesign of a real local business's site or page, clearly labeled as a concept, and share it with the owner. Get their permission before you publish anything with their name or branding. Put it all in a portfolio with a short explanation of the problem and what you built. If you don't have one yet, my post on building your first portfolio site covers it, and the one on GitHub profiles helps too. Three solid samples beat ten half-finished ones. What people want to see is that you can take a real need from idea to a working result. 6. Where to Find Your First Client Start warm, then go wider. 1. People you already know. Family, friends, classmates, teachers, club mentors. Tell them clearly what you do, and ask if they know anyone who needs it. This is how a huge number of first clients actually happen. 2. Local businesses. Walk in, message on social media, or send an email. Mention something specific you noticed, like their site loading slowly on a phone or having no online menu. 3. Communities. Student groups, local tech communities, Discord servers, and group chats. Be useful first. Answer questions, share what you're building, and let people see you're capable. 4. LinkedIn and social media. Post about your projects, share what you learn, and tell people you're open to small projects. Consistency pays off here. 5. Freelance platforms. Upwork, Fiverr, and similar sites exist, but they're crowded, and newcomers with no reviews have a tough time. They can work if you take a few small, well-scoped gigs to collect reviews, though I wouldn't make them your only plan. 7. How to Reach Out Without Being Annoying Cold messages work when they're short, specific, and easy to say yes to. Compare a lazy message with a good one. Lazy: Hi, I'm a web developer. Do you need a website? I can build anything. Better: Hi [Name], I came across [Business] while looking for [something they offer] and noticed the site is hard to use on a phone. I'm a student developer who builds simple, fast websites for local businesses. I put together a quick mockup of what a mobile-friendly version could look like. Would you like me to send it over? No pressure at all. Why the second works: It shows you actually looked at their business It names a real problem It offers something small and concrete It asks for a tiny next step, not a big commitment Send a polite follow-up after several days if you hear nothing. People are busy, and silence usually isn't a no. Don't send fifty identical messages, though. A handful of thoughtful ones beats a flood of copy-paste. 8. What to Charge This is the scary part, so let's make it simple. Don't work free forever.

articles.content: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page.

articles.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
articles.headline: Datasette-leaflet plugin fixes OpenStreetMap referrer policy
articles.summary: Datasette table pages used a no-referrer HTTP header, causing the datasette-leaflet plugin to violate OpenStreetMap's tile server policy. The plugin now sets referrer policy to strict-origin-when-cross-origin on tile requests, passing only the host rather than the full page path. The fix ensures compliance with OpenStreetMap's requirements.

articles.content: Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. The Shocking Demise of Jensen Huang. This week’s coverage was dominated, unsurprisingly, by the shocking and sudden end of Jensen Huang’s 32 year tenure as CEO of Nvidia. The end came on Thursday morning, and just a few hours later, we recorded a Sharp Tech episode recounting Huang’s legendary history, figuring out what happened, and looked forward to what this might mean for Nvidia, the tech industry, and America going forward. Also see Andrew’s view from DC, Jensen Huang Was Always Going to Lose , and listen to Wednesday’s episode of Sharp China about the geopolitical angle, and Thursday’s Dithering about both the parallels and differences between Steve Jobs and Apple. — Ben Thompson Enterprise, Consumer and Intel. The more things change, the more they stay the same: Intel remains on the back foot in the AI era, and the foundry dreams continue to flounder. On the heels of disappointing earnings and 2027 guidance that promises yet more letdowns, Ben’s Update on Wednesday examined the state of America’s would-be national champion by drawing comparisons to AMD, an Intel peer that’s red-hot right now. To understand why one company is capitalizing on skyrocketing enterprise demand while the other confronts flatlining consumer sales, the answer starts with chips chiplets and leads to more profound questions about culture, Intel’s nature, and its bifurcated strategy for the long-term (and, for subscribers, look forward to more on this topic in Sunday’s Sharp Tech mailbag episode). — Andrew Sharp And Then There’s Professional Basketball. As a palate cleanser after a week of Jensen drama, this week’s Greatest of All Talk was a look at the top and bottom of the NBA after the first three weeks. On the euphoric side of the ledger we have Warriors fans (pre-Steph injury), Lakers fans, Spurs fans, and on the other end spectrum there is nothing positive to say in Brooklyn, a familiar malaise in Cleveland, and precisely one silver lining in Salt Lake City. All of it was a great time; we also hit Adam’s experience with the NBA in Mexico City last weekend, the hardest working players in NBA history, and an anxiety-inducing conversation about the number one pick, AJ Dybantsa. — AS Presented by Agentic commerce purchases with Link, Stripe’s digital wallet that works surprisingly well for agents, grew 38x in September. The catalyst was consumer agents like Muse and Instinct. Filling out a web form is not a value-add activity for anyone. No one chooses to fill out web forms in their spare time. That’s why these agents have been particularly useful. I’ve written about how these platforms are giving ordinary people an AI agent with a computer, enabling agents to do genuinely useful things on our behalf. When one of those things is spending money, it needs a wallet that knows what it is, and isn’t, allowed to do. Stripe has learned that’s really about deciding how much freedom to give it. You might approve one purchase, or give it $500 for flights this week, and let it figure out the rest. The wallet’s job is to keep it within those lines while handling everything between “go buy this” and the purchase actually happening. That’s what Stripe is building with Link: You approve what it spends, it can come back to you if the final price changes, and eligible purchases can even come with protection if the agent makes a mistake. You can use Link on Muse, Instinct, as well as many other of the agents you might use already. articles.content: When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances. The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations generate enough text to do the job. The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the most confusion. Once we have a list of specialized vocabulary we can ask the agent to produce a glossary, with definitions for each term. Some terms may be used in different ways, in which case the LLM should provide alternative definitions, with a note as to what context the differences appear in. The LLM can be asked to follow the output format of a dictionary, with a focus on precision and conciseness. Once we have a draft glossary, then human experts in that domain should review it, and amend it for cases where the LLM has got the wrong ends of sticks. We then put the glossary somewhere where any other LLM can use it. It should be in a form that's easy for the LLM to consult, and minimize the tokens the LLM should consume in order to find meaning. We should set up a schedule to review and refresh the glossary at regular intervals, by agents and humans. We should keep it in version control, so we can see how it changes over time. Large organizations often have subtly different definitions in different places, essentially following the Domain Driven Design notion of Bounded Context . Source code can be a particularly interesting bounded context, allowing folks to understand how terminology is used within a code base. Sometimes a single glossary can span several of bounded contexts, but at other times it's better to have separate glossaries for each one, allowing LLMs to consult whichever glossaries that are relevant to what they are doing. I'd urge everyone to resist any temptation to create a single, standard, glossary - I've yet to see that work. Often the value of a glossary isn't to nail down a single definition of a term, but instead to highlight its different usage in different contexts. When there are different bounded contexts it can be interesting to compare different glossaries, or to get LLMs to compare glossaries and describe differences in usage. Comparing a source-code derived glossary to a human text can be particularly instructive. If the glossary is large, it can be worthwhile to only include the terms and links to definitions as part of the initial context. The model can then use the links for only the full definitions it needs while working. A glossary can be used in several ways within Agentic Engineering . Glossaries can inform generation of code, so that names within the generated software fit the particular vocabulary of the enterprise. Sensors in a harness can check for this usage, both in the internals of the software and in the user-interface. When generating code or documents, we may introduce new bounded contexts. For example, internal names that may be used within an organization should not be exposed in a customer-facing UI, because such internal terms are likely to be only confuse a customer. In this case a customer has a different bounded context to the part of the enterprise serving them. It's often useful for glossaries to include terms that should not be used, in which case it includes advice on what other term to use instead. Terms that are deprecated can be handled in this way, with glossary entries that indicate what period of time a term should be in effect. In my conversations with people working with agents in large organizations, a common theme is the difficulty of specialized language. This encourages the activities of domain modeling, building ontologies, and constructing explicit context layers in enterprise data . Getting LLMs to generate a glossary is a simple, but useful, part of this work. Acknowledgements Eric Nagler and Unmesh Joshi related their experiences doing this activity and thus inspired this post. Amy Pellegrini, Annie Luxton, Arun Srinivasan, Chris Ford, Daniel Terhorst-North, Dave Farley, Eric Nagler, James Shore, Jason Yip, Jimmy Nilsson, Matteo Vaccari, Michaël Le Barbier, Pete Hodgson, Pramod Sadalage, Ravi Vats, Unmesh Joshi, and Valentyn Logvynskyi commented on drafts.
