articles.title: Bliki: Generated Glossary
articles.headline: LLMs generate specialized glossaries for enterprise domains
articles.summary: When using LLMs in large organizations, specialized vocabulary foreign to the model can hinder effectiveness. The technique involves using an LLM to generate a glossary from organizational documents, emails, and chat logs, identifying terms new to the model and known terms used unfamiliar ways. Human experts review and amend the draft, which is then version-controlled and refreshed regularly. The glossary helps LLMs navigate bounded contexts, avoid exposing internal terms in customer-facing UI, and improve code generation and sensor checks within enterprise software.

articles.content: Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } }

articles.content: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation

articles.headline: Claude Fable 5.2 adds code based on ownership prompts

This behavior affects how the model handles code improvement tasks.

articles.content: Automated testing in the age of AI coding assistants is problematic: when AI agents write both production and test code, developers risk losing the assurance that automated tests protect against functional errors. Matteo Vaccari makes three claims: (1) when AI writes the code, developers become its customers; (2) therefore customer tests, not developer tests, become the primary contract between humans and AI; (3) moving that contract into test data rather than test code makes it easier to protect it from unexpected modifications by coding agents. All of this optimizes for human-readable tests that establish a contract between humans and AI. While in the past DSL parsers and custom test runners were expensive to write and maintain, now AI makes them cheap. more…
articles.excerpt: Automated testing in the age of AI coding assistants is problematic: when AI agents write both production and test code, developers risk losing the assurance that automated tests protect against functional errors.
articles.title: Tests as data: ensuring AI-generated code does what we want
articles.headline: AI coding agents generate tests developers can't trust
articles.summary: When AI writes both production and test code, developers lose confidence in automated tests. Interviews with 26 developers reveal they stop trusting tests as AI refactors both code and tests. AI-generated tests often use heavy mocks that break on harmless refactoring, proving implementation details rather than correct behavior. Moving tests to data files, rather than code, makes them easier to protect from unexpected AI modifications while remaining human-readable. This approach optimizes for a contract between humans and AI, ensuring tests specify correct behavior rather than confirming buggy implementation.

articles.content: Listen to this post: Good morning, This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Roblox CEO David Baszucki . I’ve interviewed Baszucki twice, in February 2022 , and November 2023 . What struck me about this interview is just how much AI has changed the landscape for Roblox. This was a company predicated on the concept that anyone can make a game, but now, for the first time, literally anyone can make a game. That means a world of abundance, and in that world, there is an opportunity to be an Aggregator, and Roblox is aggressively pursuing that opportunity. To that end, we discuss how AI has changed Baszucki’s view of what is possible, what goes into a game creation harness, making games on your phone, and the power of recommendation. Then we talk about Roblox’s vision of a universal player, where a Roblox game works everywhere, and Roblox Everywhere, where Roblox developers can use the platform beyond the Roblox app. We also touch on advertising — the natural Aggregator business model — and whether Baszucki still thinks he is building the metaverse. As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player. On to the Interview: An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: The AI Impact | A Game Creation Harness | Roblox Build | Roblox Discovery | Universal Player | Roblox Everywhere | Advertising | Metaverses The AI Impact David Baszucki, welcome back to Stratechery. DB: Thank you, Ben, for having me back. It’s great to be here. So this is the third time I’ve interviewed you, and I want to sort of put that in an interesting context. First, you started Roblox in 2004, you went public in 2021, you first talked to me in 2022 and again in 2023 , that’s like a nearly 20-year stretch. Now it’s 2026, and here’s my question: Is the world more different for you now, compared to three years before, than it was for the entire first two decades from starting the company to the last time we talked? DB: The changes in the world we all feel are sure happening a lot more rapidly. When we first published Roblox — I don’t know if people on this podcast remember — software used to be distributed on floppy disks and CDs. You know, the funny thing is, you’re the second person I’ve interviewed in the last two or three weeks where we’ve referenced back to fact that the reason we say packaged software is it used to actually be packaged! DB: It’s been crazy, we had the Internet, when we started the company, we had the vision of a category called immersive co-experience, sci-fi writers have been writing about the holodeck forever, and we went along our way. I’m still pro-metaverse, we can use the word metaverse, it’s okay. DB: Okay, good, we use them all. It’s Snow Crash — metaverse, holodeck, they’re all good. We started on this vision of building human co-experience, we saw the mobile age come across us, we saw the crypto age. The AI acceleration wave we’re in is faster and bigger and crazier than anything I’ve ever seen, it’s changing how we think about the product, it’s changing how people are going to create games. What’s really exciting is, when we started the company, we had this slogan called “You Make the Game”. Yep. DB: We started with that slogan, we learned along the way that the ratio of people who might want to play games to make games has drifted — more people want to just play games than make games, because historically making games has been Roblox Studio and 3D editing and writing script. We could be approaching the time where “You Make the Game” really comes true, and where making a game is accessible to everyone. It’s really fun, I’ll tell you a bit about some of the experiments we’ve been having with Roblox Build . But we’re entering an era where making a game could be as big as playing a game. I’m right there with you. We’re obviously going to touch on all those points, I think it’s probably predictable what we want to talk about. But to go back to 2023, you called AI then, “a super paintbrush and a super 3D modeler, rather than a full replacement” — Is that still how you’re thinking about AI? DB: It’s what the data is proving out. We just had our earnings call a few weeks ago , we highlighted a lot of acceleration. One, there’s various ways humans can augment with AI on Roblox, they can use MCP , which is like plugging in a model, they can use the Roblox AI assistant to help build. And what do you mean with that MCP server? You mentioned you had 5x growth quarter-over-quarter. That’s where you’re actually using Claude Code or Codex or whatever to work with Roblox? DB: People are plugging in, we can see all of them — Claude Code, Codex, other models — all being plugged into Roblox Studio to help build things. We’ve seen two games hit the top 20 made by AI, we have other metrics like the number of assets. What do you mean by “made by AI”? Because you also said 80% of games in the top 100 have AI-contributed content. DB: Touched by AI, vibe-coded directly with AI, and we can see the count of assets accelerating. Got it. DB: It’s turned out to be, I believe, somewhat faithful to what I said. This is a human paintbrush accelerator, good ideas are still very important, novel types of gameplay are very important. But people are able to flex their creativity much more quickly.

articles.title: An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play
articles.headline: Roblox CEO says AI enables anyone to make games, targets aggregation
articles.summary: Roblox CEO David Baszucki says AI has made game creation accessible to everyone for the first time, citing 5x quarter-over-quarter growth in AI-assisted development and 80% of top-100 games now containing AI-contributed content. The company is pursuing an aggregation business model through AI-powered tools like Roblox Build, aiming to make game creation as common as gameplay while supporting a universal player experience across devices.

articles.content: Before we start, I’d like to share some exciting news: The Pragmatic Summit is returning! It’s a one-day event on 10 February in San Francisco, almost exactly one year after the first Summit. I’ll be hosting and the first few speakers are confirmed. Some faces may be familiar to regular readers and listeners! My goal with the Summit is to make it the single best event for connecting with like-minded engineering leaders and engineers, and curious, driven people. Feedback from last year was that it was the attendees and the quality of debate that made it a standout event. We aim to deliver the same this time with the organizing team, including space for roundtable discussions, and talking with speakers who can stay around after their talk. The Pragmatic Engineer team shall be there too. Applications are open : this summit is for senior+ engineers and engineering leaders who are shaping how modern engineering teams build software, ship products, and scale up to meet challenging demand curves. Tickets are priced at $1,000. You can check out last year’s talks , or watch a one-minute video summary. This year’s Summit is made possible by friends at WorkOS , which is helping organize the event and is the exclusive sponsor. Thank you! I hope to see many of you there! Now, onto today’s article. Sean Allen is a software engineer with deep expertise in building large distributed systems, stream processing, and confidential computing. He is a core contributor to the programming language Pony , which is designed for concurrency. Sean is a distinguished engineer at Antithesis. I was keen to talk with Sean due to his work on confidential computing at Microsoft, as well as his extensive work on the Pony language, and his passion for software correctness, which he works on fulltime at Antithesis. For this conversation, we set ourselves the challenge of discussing modern software engineering without using the phrase “AI” a single time. Read on to see if it’s possible in 2026… In this article, the questions are posed by me in bold font, with Sean’s words in normal font. Today we cover: Software correctness & languages built for correctness. Why languages in the Meta Language (ML) family that are built around strong type systems catch more errors during compilation time than those in the Algorithmic Language (ALGOL) family. Does anybody care about testing? For someone passionate about correctness, Sean is surprisingly anti-testing. He argues that manual testing is the worst way to ensure correctness because you want illegal states to be prohibited from being expressed in a language – even before testing. Workloads & correctness. A more robust way of testing stuff than things like unit tests, is to define “workloads” that can be executed numerous times during a test. A common workload example is The Bank Test to stress test database isolation guarantees. Is quality a “gate” or not? It’s tempting to think of quality checks as closed gates that keep out poor quality. Sean pushes back against this; he says it’s important to consider quality from the very start, and to build with validation techniques that provide feedback on correctness. He prefers this to adding CI/CD quality “gates” late in the development process. Tech debt only hurts if you have to pay it back. Stop being afraid of tech debt because you often don’t need to pay it back at all! Sean says it’s common that tech debt is disregarded during rewrites when a system has become popular. No good fix for supply chain security. Supply chain attacks – when a package gets hijacked by an attacker and malicious code is executed on a machine or service – are very hard to defend against because languages with truly robust defenses, like ‘E’, are unpopular, while popular languages assume a trustworthy ecosystem. There’s no single or simple fix, says Sean. Garbage collection is slow – but doesn’t have to be. A summary of why garbage collection is devastating for runtime performance, and how Sean built a predictably performant approach in the Pony language. Go slow to go fast. Counter-intuitive advice: spend more time designing upfront and aligning everyone, and then you’ll move fast! You can also watch this conversation on YouTube : An amusing detail: Sean and I discovered we share in common a first fulltime employer. We both worked at a company called ‘Sense/Net’ at the start of our careers, although they were totally separate businesses in different countries. The founders of each must’ve been fans of the foundational cyberpunk novel, ‘Neuromancer’ by William Gibson, where the ‘Sense/Net’ name comes from . Note: Antithesis is a podcast sponsor, but this deepdive is not sponsored by them. I’ve just been thinking a lot more about software correctness in the context of AI agents producing more code than ever, thereby creating opportunities for more bugs to ship to prod than ever. I wanted to learn more about this from an engineer with extensive experience in this area. 1. Software correctness & languages built for correctness Gergely: How do you define ‘software correctness’? Sean: “It’s down to whether my program does what I expect. I tend to talk about things in terms of ‘invariants,’ which is a more formal specification term. An invariant is a guarantee that my software does what’s expected of it. But here’s the problem: in lots of cases, people don’t know what they expect their software to do upfront! They know when it’s not working, but they don’t necessarily know what it means for it to be working. ‘Correct’ software does its business purpose and doesn’t wake anybody up at 2 a.m. with an outage. That is correct enough for me.” Your personal definition of ‘beautiful code’ mirrors this. Sean: “I was on the CoRecursive podcast when the subject of beautiful code in Ruby came up. I didn’t really know what people meant when they said ‘beautiful code’.

articles.title: Software correctness & supply chain security, with Sean Allen
articles.headline: Sean Allen discusses software correctness and supply chain security at Antithesis
articles.summary: Sean Allen, a core contributor to the Pony language and distinguished engineer at Antithesis, discusses software correctness, arguing that languages with strong type systems catch more errors at compilation. He critiques manual testing, advocates for defining workloads to stress test systems, and warns that supply chain attacks are difficult to defend against in popular languages. Allen also explains how the Pony language addresses garbage collection performance and advises spending more time on upfront design to reduce technical debt.

articles.content: Release: llm-gemini 0.37 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family. It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme: Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen $1.50 $0.075 $7.50 Carbon and Argon are the same price , and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task. Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that. I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans . Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels: Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark. Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models: In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

articles.content: It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar. The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends . One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent. Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on? Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Ben Thompson’s Stratechery newsletter reflects on the recent election’s impact on data centers . I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite. He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI: you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race. There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition. He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming. There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments. To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve been a long-time fan of Hadley Wickham, for how he has tamed the rather messy world of R programming into a well-designed tidyverse . He is another thoughtful voice to listen to as we move into the world of agentic engineering , in this case by trying to figure out what the real cost of tokens is . I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data? His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.) ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ There’s a creepy excitement at the thought that models are clever enough to edit the weights of models, an activity that Takehi et al refer to as Weight-Space Programming . Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

articles.content: Long-horizon agents can automate complex tasks that take days or weeks to complete and involve multiple exchanges with people and external systems. Many things can go wrong during this time, including process crashes, network failures, and unanticipated real-world behavior. Kiran Prakash explains durable execution: an emerging pattern that helps agents recover from these failures and move towards their goal. In this programming model, the runtime keeps a record of the result of each step that interacts with the outside world so that, when a failure occurs, the program runs again, completed steps are skipped, and the program's state is rebuilt from the record. more…

The runtime records each step's result, allowing the program to rebuild state from the record when failures occur, making previously uneconomical work viable for enterprises.

articles.content: Listen and watch now on YouTube , Apple , and Spotify . See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom. Brought to You by • turbopuffer – The tpuf eng team is completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles. And they’re documenting all of it! They made epic progress; take a look: turbopuffer.com/v3 • Antithesis – use AI agents to work on critical systems without worrying about correctness. Antithesis runs your complete system in a hostile environment, analyzes its behavior, and reproduces every issue perfectly. Learn more • Entire – Entire launched its own Git forge, shipped Continuous Memory , and reinvented the pull request (called Trails ). Trails are a much more natural workflow when agents keep pushing new changes, after iterating on feedback – and you have more context and control on when a change is ready to merge. Check it out In this episode What is involved in scaling up large, popular products at places like Slack and GitHub? We get an insider’s view on this from Maude Lemaire , a principal engineer and author of ‘ Refactoring at Scale: Regaining Control of Your Codebase .’ She spent nearly eight years at Slack, where she led the backend performance infrastructure team, before joining GitHub to tackle database scaling challenges. Most recently, she worked on improving performance at Cursor – including time to first token. In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer , Maude and I dig into the challenges of scaling some of the world’s largest software products. We explore how Slack handled growing numbers of enterprise customers, how it evolved its approach to load testing, and the lessons Maude learned during nearly eight years of scaling Slack’s infrastructure. She also tells us what it was like joining GitHub in 2024 when Copilot was taking off, the challenges of working with GitHub’s gigantic Rails monolith, and how Maude uses AI in her work – while keeping judgment calls and decision-making firmly in her own hands. Takeaways from the conversation with Maude Here are eight interesting points from our discussion: 1. Performance should matter even if there’s no competition. In 2015, the homepage of Rent the Runway took up to 10 seconds to fully load due to a high-resolution hero image on the site. Maude was told it wasn’t an issue because there were no competitors to worry about. She thought differently: “The best competition is competition with yourself, knowing that you can do better, knowing that you can drive a better experience, ” she said. Maude spent some free time on speeding up the website without asking for permission to do so because it was the right call. 2. Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid thundering herds. Here’s an example of a thundering herd : the CEO of a 100,000-member Slack channel posts “everyone gets Friday off!” In response, people start posting custom emojis – hundreds of them. The problem is that every single custom emoji has to fan out to all 100,000 users. With 10 custom emojis, that’s 1,000,000 fan-outs, with 100 it’s 10,000,000; a lot of network load! Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid this problem. In reality, the absent 24th custom emoji is not missed. 3. Event floods can cripple the machines of Slack’s power users. Event floods are the cousin of thundering herds: they occur when a single client is overwhelmed by events coming through its own WebSocket. For example, when an IT worker is logged into lots of busy channels and they all receive the “everyone gets Friday off!” message – along with all the associated custom emojis and messages. This “power user” gets a sudden influx of messages with no deduplication and they struggle. 4. Load testing 500,000 WebSocket connections the simple way would have cost $150,000 per run. A new customer with 500,000 users was about to sign up to Slack, and Maude needed to run a load test to confirm the service could handle the load. Initially, she planned to spin up headless Chrome instances – each instance running a Slack session, and that would have cost $0.37 per five-hour session, per instance. The total price would’ve been crazily expensive. Instead, Maude built a tool called Koi Pond that spins up slimmed-down versions of Slack (‘Koi’), written in Go to establish the WebSocket connections. 5. Active Record downside: too much database load! GitHub used to be a Ruby on Rails monolith, which used Active Record as a database abstraction layer. This caused unexpected load: GitHub’s home page fetched live data from the database for most reloads, and loading the home page regularly triggered 100 SQL queries across three database clusters. This revealed a downside of abstractions like Active Record to Maude: when devs used it, they didn’t know or care about the additional load they unwittingly placed on the database while fetching data for whatever they were working on. 6. GitHub could not add more than 16 database shards because of scatter query problems. A scatter query is one without a primary key (a sharding key), and it needs to be run across all shard instances . But more shards make such queries slower. Back in the day at GitHub, lots of queries made through Active Record (many on the homepage) were scatter queries. This limitation prevented GitHub from adding more than 16 shards. I find this detail fascinating: it shows why a developer-friendly abstraction (Active Record) can actually cause severe pain at the infra level! 7. For platform work, Maude personally verifies everything she gets from an LLM. When doing foundational work, Maude pays close attention to verifying the output of LLMs because she believes that ambitious structures can only be built on stable foundations. It’s an interesting approach to separate “foundational” and “non-foundational” work in order to give more attention to the former, most critical, type. 8. Platform and product engineers should rotate more.

articles.content: Release: llm 0.37.2 Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w . LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers. Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1 .

articles.title: llm 0.37.2
articles.headline: LLM 0.37.2 released to fix critical security vulnerability
articles.summary: LLM version 0.37.2 was released to fix a security vulnerability reported by Daniel de Araujo. The issue allowed configured OpenAI API keys to be accidentally sent to other OpenAI-compatible API providers when using specific model configurations. The vulnerability was triggered if an API key had never been stored or if a model with responses: true was run with chat_completions enabled. The update introduces the llm openai endpoint add command for safer management of compatible endpoints.

articles.content: Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

articles.content: Before we start: I’m in San Francisco this week and there are a few remaining spots for these live events (registration required): Wednesday (4 Nov): The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged at the iconic SFJAZZ Center. With Diogo Almeida (creator of Jev & co-inventor of ChatGPT), and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO of Oxide). Thursday (5 Nov): System Update at The Howard SF. With Karri Saarinen (Linear), Kath Korevec (OpenAI), David Cramer (Sentry) and Adam Rogal (DoorDash) Also, this week there will be no issue of The Pulse on Thursday. Regular scheduling returns next week! In September, when The Pragmatic Engineer turned five , I announced an essay challenge, inviting readers to write about how things have changed in tech workplaces and in our projects, for the chance to win a grand prize of $10,000 awarded to our favorite article. We received 125 submissions, covering a wide range of viewpoints and experiences. Many thanks to everyone who took part. In today’s issue, we publish the winning piece in full. Congratulations to software engineer Neil Kakkar ! We appreciate the sheer volume of data that Neil has collected about how his own output has changed over time. Neil is a dev based in London, with nine years of professional experience; he has interned at Google, and been a software engineer at Bloomberg, Posthog, and Tano. His previous workplace, PostHog, is an open source project, which must’ve been useful for gathering historic data. In a follow-up issue, we’ll highlight runner-up essays, and link to the ones that impressed us for the effort on show and interesting thoughts. With that, it’s over to Neil. He covers: Two eras of shipping . Until last year, he was merging between eight and 20 pull requests (PRs) per month. But since joining an AI-native startup, Neil now ships 200+ PRs per month, approximately a tenfold increase. Old constraints that disappeared. No more communications overhead or code reviews. The tradeoff: moving faster and breaking things. New constraints that appeared. Too much context switching (thrashing), losing shared context, pacing yourself is harder, less focus on design, and worries about AI plan limits. How AI is changing software engineering. Everyone needs to be onboard with AI to get the benefits at work, encouraging experimentation makes a difference, and many existing technologies and processes crack under the change. I’ve been working at an AI native startup for the past eight months. Before joining Tano , I was at PostHog for four years, a fast moving pre-AI startup, and started my career at Bloomberg , a big fintech private company, where I spent three years. All three workplaces are different: Bloomberg is huge, with 20,000 people and very defined processes. PostHog is smaller, at around 10 people when I joined, and now at 200. At Tano, I was the first engineer and we’re now around 10 people in total. In each job, I’ve seen what a difference speed and culture make, and more recently, how culture needs to change to keep up with AI. To back things up, I use in-depth stats about my work at PostHog and Tano. I also have some very rough numbers from Bloomberg. By far, I’ve written more code and made a lot more PRs at Tano than I did at PostHog, and a major part of this is down to AI. Facilitating the shift is engineering culture. One disclaimer before we get into it: the PostHog stats are from pre-AI. I’ve been following their journey, and PostHog is as “AI-pilled” as it gets now, and output is increasing significantly. In this article, I treat it as a ‘pre-AI baseline’ for excellent engineering work. Tano is a fast-moving AI-native startup, founded after AI agents emerged. 1. Two eras of shipping Let’s start with some raw numbers. I’m shipping 11x more PRs at Tano than at PostHog, where I shipped 2.4x as many as I did at Bloomberg. At Bloomberg, I was just starting my career, so I wasn’t the fastest, and moving to PostHog opened my eyes to what a fast-moving startup culture really looks like: we were encouraged to take responsibility, ship things quickly, listen to customers, and solve their issues ASAP. At Bloomberg and PostHog there was a high bar for code: everything had to be peer reviewed, and as I became senior, I spent a big chunk of my time reviewing code. PRs can be an easily gamed metric, but I was not trying to game the numbers, so they’re an honest representation of the work done. Below are details of everything I worked on to justify the 11x PR multiplier. What I worked on I joined PostHog as a full stack software engineer and worked across the product, from the ingestion pipeline to optimising our analytics queries for funnels and retention on Clickhouse, scaling it up to handle a billion+ events scale, and eventually building out the experimentation product from scratch. I later led the Feature Success team, where we built out two new products: surveys and early access features, while improving experimentation and feature flags. I joined Tano as a founding engineer and focused on a similar breadth of product as at PostHog, but all compressed into eight months instead of 45. I built out our new affiliate platform, made our content monitoring system a lot more efficient, and did some big migrations, like moving the entire agent architecture to a new system with persistent memory, better tools, and superior observability. Here’s a summary of work I did at both companies: How I work today At PostHog until late 2024, the extent of AI was tab completion. It was great for automating menial work like repetitive test cases, but was a long way away from today’s autonomous agents that can build an entire feature with no human input. When I joined Tano this year, Claude Code Desktop was already present with really good agent support, and could build out entire features with little hand-holding.

articles.content: Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. AI on the Ballot. This week’s elections delivered Democrats the largest Congressional majority either party has enjoyed in 36 years, and coupled with a variety of similar results at the state level (particularly in Texas), not to mention plenty of data center opposition among Republicans, the future of the AI buildout is now fraught with more regulatory uncertainty than ever. I wrote about X, 2024 symmetry, and the more political aspects of the election for Sharp Text , while Ben’s Article on Wednesday built on his data center warnings from April and provided 10 takes on the post-midterms landscape for tech companies. — Andrew Sharp A Google State of the Union. Last week Google reported earnings and saw growth in search revenue slow for the first time in five quarters. Given the appearance of mortality in what might be the greatest business in the history of digital commerce, investors were predictably spooked. However, I think the company deserves time to see if AI Mode ends up like Stories and Reels did for Facebook: if anyone can monetize AI with ads, it’s going to be Google. On Sharp Tech , we also got into why Google’s AI bet is about more than AI Mode, and why I find myself impressed by Google’s fortitude, even if the rest of the Internet is a casualty. — Ben Thompson And What About China? Elections have consequences, as they say, so what might a Democratic Congressional majority mean for the next two years of U.S.-China relations? We tried to answer that question on Sharp China this week , including predicting factional foreign policy fights between the left and center-left, highlighting the profound unknowns concerning President Trump’s posture after this week’s defeat, and offering one safe bet in the new environment: life is about to get a lot more complicated for Jensen Huang in Washington. — AS Presented by I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy. Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating. Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them. Stratechery Articles and Updates Google Earnings, Facebook Déjà Vu, The Agent Play — Google’s earnings miss looks a lot like Facebook’s, and that’s a credit to Google. The company is being more aggressive than they get credit for. Apple Earnings, Memory Problems, The Hardware Company Regression — Apple’s earnings suggest that the company’s hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt? AI on the Ballot — Data Centers were on the ballot, and they lost in a major way; what does it mean if American opposition to building is permanent? An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI — An interview with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi about the working for one of tech’s oldest software companies, and how Intuit is leaning into the AI paradigm shift. Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp X Marks the Rot — Republicans colonized Twitter and then cannibalized their support with two years of memes, corruption and excess. Dithering with Ben Thompson and Daring Fireball’s John Gruber DoorDash and Google The MacBook Pro (with touch) Asianometry with Jon Yu The Rise of GLM and China’s Zhipu AI Sharp China with Andrew Sharp and Sinocism’s Bill Bishop Parsing the Fifth Plenum; US-China After the Midterms; New Scrutiny for Nvidia?; Cybersecurity and Espionage Greatest of All Talk The Rapture and the Wild West, Luka Doncic on Praise Probation, AJ Dybantsa Saves the Wizards Sharp Tech with Andrew Sharp and Ben Thompson Subscriber Mail: Apple Past and Present, Omarchy, Instacart, and Baseball America Votes Against Data Centers, Implications for Big Tech and Beyond, Were Google Bears Right All Along? articles.content: Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion ,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.) Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 1 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 2 Authors should fill the prose themselves. Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress. In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then? Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease . I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom. A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM. There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 3 . Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose. Notes 1: Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up. 2: My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source). 3: Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.” Acknowledgements Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on drafts of this post. I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

articles.title: Bliki: LLM Voice
articles.headline: Fowler warns against LLM prose causing uncanny valley reaction
articles.summary: Martin Fowler warns that LLM-generated prose triggers an uncanny valley reaction, making readers uncomfortable. He advises authors against using LLMs to draft writing, even when edited, as the LLM voice is hard to remove. Fowler notes the issue matters for regular communicators and acknowledges legitimate uses for those with disabilities or language barriers, but emphasizes human writing is essential for clear thinking and communication.

articles.content: Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember.

The model sits on the efficiency frontier, providing competitive performance per task cost compared to higher-priced alternatives like Claude Fable.

articles.content: TL;DR Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production. I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance? The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is. Building it right Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right . It’s pretty much our default way of working and thinking and it’s where many of the practices and technologies we invented and championed came from. We want software that is useful and helpful, can be changed next year, and doesn’t fall over in production. Our developers adopted, championed or invented some of the first versions of continuous integration, pairing, automated testing, continuous delivery, microservices and many others early because they helped us build the software right. Early coding agents made it very easy to produce code, including code we wouldn’t have wanted anywhere near production, written by people who have not learned about the chasm between building something and making it run in production safely. The tools have improved enormously, but experienced developers still have questions. Are we confident this is the right behaviour? Does it work as expected? Are these the right boundaries? Will we be able to evolve it? Does it abide by the principles and practices we learned the hard way to give us confidence it will meet the needs of the customer and stay up in production? What happens when something fails? Will another team be able to live with it? And so on. Underneath all of those sits a bigger question. How much can we trust a system when nobody has experience of building it this way? Let me state that another way. Nearly every system we have in production now was built the old way, by hand, by people we could trust (hopefully). Everything we build now is the new way and we have not lived with that yet. After more than 25 years in technology, I’ve come to value the judgment people develop through experience. I regularly put similar questions to models and to senior technologists at Thoughtworks. For the difficult questions, I still get more useful answers from the humans or maybe more insightful with very specific experience that helps me better understand the point. They challenge the premise, recognise a pattern from something that went wrong ten years ago, or spot the organisational problem hiding inside the technical one. I can now access an extraordinary amount of information. I still need people who can help me think through what matters, I still need wisdom and insight. That type judgment is exactly what hesitant experienced developers are trying to protect. And I want to be clear: they are not hesitant to use a coding assistant, they are hesitant to go all in and let the agents do all the execution. They are hesitant to take their hand off the wheel because they don’t have full confidence the agents have the right guardrails in place to run off on their own. A week at the whiteboard Recently, Giles Alexander, our Regional CTO for Europe, brought senior engineers, infrastructure consultants and product people together for a week of working in exactly this way. No code written by anyone. Everything built by agents. The point wasn’t to prove that an airline application could be built in a week. (Funnily enough they got 80% done and we all know what that means… you can’t make stuff up!) The purpose of the experiment was to learn what happens to the team’s work when agents do all of the coding. You can read some of what they learned here . What struck me in our conversations was how much time they spent at the whiteboard. Working out the domain. Drawing boundaries. Deciding what should happen next and making plans the agents could act on. Meanwhile, the agents kept producing code beyond the team’s working day. The humans were also designing the feedback around that work: tests, contracts, architecture checks and a delivery pipeline. They were working out how to give agents enough freedom to make progress while keeping confidence in the result. Most of the work at the keyboard was directing agents to put this learning into the harness, so the building and testing agents got it right on the next run and they could have more confidence in what they built. Interestingly in the end the product person committed more feature code than anyone else on the team. When I asked them to estimate they said they spend about ⅔ of their time at the whiteboard and ⅓ on the harness, which could give us some clue as to how developers will work in the future, but before you get ahead of yourself redesigning your team, that’s not the end of the story… The application ran. The build was red. The application ran, but the build was frequently red. It worked on their machine - again you couldn’t make this up if you tried! A constant red build gives me the ick. A red build should mean something: stop, investigate, fix it.

articles.title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?
articles.headline: Experienced developers wary of agentic development due to production readiness concerns
articles.summary: Thoughtworks CTO Rachel Laycock explains why senior developers hesitate to fully adopt agentic development. Despite rapid code generation, teams worry about trust, boundaries, and the gap between building and running software safely. An experiment building an airline application entirely with agents revealed that humans spent significant time at whiteboards defining domains and designing feedback mechanisms like tests and pipelines. The application frequently had red builds, raising concerns about CI/CD reliability and the ability to spot real failures. The experiment highlights the need for new practices to manage batch sizes and ensure stability as AI adoption increases.

Brought to You by • turbopuffer – The tpuf eng team is completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles. And they’re documenting all of it! They made epic progress, take a look: turbopuffer.com/v3 • Linear – one of the big challenges for us devs is the sheer amount of code to review. Linear Diffs is a new feature to review PRs inside of Linear, with all the context in one place. It also supports stacked PRs. Check it out • WorkOS – WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent + your rules and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human. Works with Claude Code, Codex & MCP gateways. Give it a spin In this episode An engineer who helped create today’s software engineering curriculum now says to burn down almost all of it. What’s the cause of this contradiction? We find out from the lead author of Software Engineering at Google . Titus Winters spent more than a decade at Google, where he led its readability program and built Abseil , Google’s open-sourced foundational C++ libraries. He is currently a Senior Principal Scientist at Adobe, where he focuses on developer experience and productivity. In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast , Titus and I discuss how his team tackled a massive refactoring project across Google’s 250-million-line C++ codebase, why Google made testing mandatory, and his work on updating the ACM/IEEE undergraduate computer science curriculum guidelines. We also explore why traditional productivity metrics miss some of AI’s biggest benefits, what needs to change in CS education, and how new engineers can stand out. Takeaways from the conversation with Titus Titus is a deep thinker and has worked on some very interesting projects. Here are 12 things that stick out to me from our chat. 1. Was refactoring 250M+ lines of C++ code the largest refactoring task of all time? This happened at Google in 2010, a few months after Titus joined the search giant. An internal email asked for volunteers to help clean up old C++ code, some of it written by the very first Googlers. A team of a dozen people was assembled. Google had close to 250M lines of code at the time, edited by 10,000 engineers. Titus recalled the cleanup: “We were replacing the foundation of the Empire State Building. We were not allowed to close the building or block traffic. Oh, and we discovered nuclear waste in the basement.” 2. The refactoring was done with advanced language parsing techniques, long before LLMs existed. Back in 2010, there were no LLMs for this giant refactor. Here’s what the team did: Parse : ran a MapReduce over the whole codebase. The mapper parsed every build target into an abstract syntax tree Match : match exact call patterns in the tree Code generation: generated edits to be made by the machine Coexist : make the old API and new API work side-by-side Shard : once the new API is ready to go, split the edits by directory, and send them out in batches Block the old: make sure nobody copied the old pattern back into the code Delete : remove the old API The clang-format toolkit exists because Titus and his team needed it for this refactor. 3. Google made automated tests mandatory after Search could no longer ship regularly. Around 2007, Search, the flagship product, was unable to ship at a monthly cadence any more, and the best they could ship to production was quarterly. Almost every change at Google touched Search’s code, even things like a change to Gmail. To clamp down, Google, as an org, mandated that every change was to be accompanied by a test. Over time, Search returned to its former higher cadence. 4. Google’s readability program might have been the largest educational program ever in tech. To make a code change at Google, two people need to sign off that change through a code review: An “owner” of the file/project: someone on the team with domain knowledge A “readability” reviewer: an engineer certified to be a “readability” expert in the given language that the change was made in Google’s first engineer, Craig Silverstein, walked each new dev hire through their first change. Java teams turned this approach into mentoring, where experienced reviewers were assigned to review all changes in a round-robin fashion. And soon enough, a formalized readability program was built for all languages. When Titus left Google three months ago, 10,000+ engineers were enrolled in readability at any given time. Has there ever been a bigger engineering “classroom” anywhere else? 5. Fear is not an acceptable basis for engineering. Titus believes your codebase is unsustainable if it’s not possible to make a valuable change safely. There shouldn’t be fear about making a change to a codebase. Having the right “security nets” that catch errors is strategically very valuable because it enables teams to make changes without fear. 6. With AI, outages seem to be going up. Titus talks to engineers at other companies and it’s the same picture: code output is up hugely versus a year ago, and outages are also up about 30%, while the number of features shipped is static. It seems like treading water.

articles.content: Listen to this post: Good morning, This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi . Goodarzi took a very non-traditional path to Silicon Valley, joining Intuit in 2004 after working at Siemens and Honeywell. After managing business units across the company he became CEO in 2019, and is taking on the challenge of figuring out how one of tech’s oldest software companies manages the AI paradigm shift. In this interview we discuss Goodarzi’s background and the what it takes to be an effective generalist, and get his take on how Intuit has thrived for 44 years. We discuss the shift from Quicken to Quickbooks, the TurboTax business, and how Goodarzi thinks about the consumer space today. Then we talk about accountants, Intuit’s most important customer acquisition channel, and how the company wants to change the profession from partners to customers via AI. I present the case to Goodarzi that Intuit seems like its being disrupted, and he makes the case why they are well positioned to actual grow their market. We also touch on acquisitions like Credit Karma and Mailchimp, and how Intuit has managed business model changes in the past, and what needs to change in the future. As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player. On to the Interview: An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: Being a Generalist | Intuit History | TurboTax and Credit Karma | The Future of Accountants | Disruption | Mailchimp | Intuit’s AI Future Being a Generalist Sasan Goodarzi, welcome to Stratechery. Sasan Goodarzi: Thank you for having me, I’m a big fan of all the work that you do. It’s great to be a part of it. Well, we’ll get to my relationship with Intuit, which I’ve had for many years. Big fan? I’m going to have to think about that one. We are here to talk about Intuit, a company that you have been at, with a brief break, for over 20 years. Before we get to that, however, tell me about your background, which is a very interesting one. Let’s start with where you were born. SG: Yes, I was born in Tehran, in Iran, and I am the youngest of three — 13 years younger than the other two brothers. I was told I was special, I think I was an accident, so there you go. And back then, you’d ship your kids to the U.S. because everybody wanted to come to the U.S. to study and so my brothers were in the U.S. already studying, and my parents decided to do an experiment with me and shipped me to the U.S. at the age of nine and I was very fortunate, because the revolution actually happened. Got it. So you had already left before then, I wasn’t quite sure on that timing. SG: Yeah, yeah. I was very fortunate, I left before the revolution, about eight to nine months before the revolution, and have been in the U.S. ever since. Where did you end up in the U.S.? SG: I came to Orlando, Florida of all places, because my brothers were going to the University of Central Florida. And, by the way, back then we used to say, “U Can’t Finish”, that’s what we called it, but it’s a great university. But anyways, for that reason, I was in Orlando until my early 20s, until I started being moved by Honeywell. Every couple of years, I was going to a different state, which was a lot of fun, and eventually ended up in California. You studied electrical engineering, right? And then you were at Honeywell and Invensys. What were you doing there? I mean, it doesn’t seem quite the obvious path to being CEO of Intuit, to say the least. SG: Not at all. In fact, it’s advice I give, career advice I give to folks. I actually started at Siemens, I was a technical marketing person, which really — I don’t know why they called it marketing, it was all a technical role that supported our field sales folks. I was in the power generation business unit at Siemens so I used to go pitch why our power generation was better than anybody else’s. I don’t think they need much marketing these days in the Siemens Power Generation Unit. SG: (laughing) Yeah that’s right, they don’t. I did that for four years and frankly, I didn’t know what I wanted to do with my life, because in the meantime, I was doing startups on the side. In fact, before I even started at Siemens, I did a startup called Lazer Cables — with, at that time, a very good friend that was actually the genius behind the idea of fiber optics for the music industry, so I was dabbling in a lot of different stuff. When I was at Siemens, I love the company, but I was wondering, “Is the corporate world cut out for me?”, and I got recruited to Honeywell. And at Honeywell, they put me — it was like business development. In essence, they put me in charge of something they were experimenting with, which was just down my alley, because it was, in essence, a startup as part of Honeywell and I fell in love with the company because of that. I was there, I think like eight years. So is this — was this going to different states? Was that because Honeywell, being a defense contractor, they just have to source from everywhere? Is that the connection? SG: Yeah, but I was in the industrial home automation division.

articles.content: Andrej Karpathy sees a widening gap in how people see LLM capabilities. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Many of my colleagues are living in a world where LLM capabilities are stunning, but it’s easy to forget that’s not what most people experience. One thing I do is use free-tier LLM chatbots, and I’m still finding that while most of the time they are useful, their unreliability undermines much of that usefulness. Yes, you can argue that I’m not using frontier tools or a forceful enough harness, but that’s true of most regular folks too. To understand their perception, it’s handy to experience it. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ That observation particularly resonates with me today, as I’ve just spent the weekend at Foocamp, an open space event run by O’Reilly. It was full of those who are experiencing that vertigo of LLM capabilities, so it felt very much like being in a bubble of those on the bleeding edge. While it’s worth remembering that that’s not a typical view of what’s happening, it’s good to see what those explorers are experiencing. (As I talk about this, I’m applying the Chatham House rule , if anyone wants attribution, let me know.) A couple of folks talked about doing immersion courses to help teach developers how to do agentic engineering . The idea is to get people out of their usual work environment, and spend one or two weeks with experienced coaches, learning how to use these tools well. Such things remind me very much of the Extreme Programming immersion classes I was involved with at the turn of the century. As with that, the experience of building something is important to understand such a new style of work. Unsurprisingly the coaches observed that the biggest impact wasn’t technical, but emotional. New tools are just new tools, but these tools change basic assumptions of what it means to be a software developer, which for many people challenges their identity. One coach said how his main job was to take such people out for a walk to a coffee shop, so they could process what’s happening. (This reminds me of a participant of the Extreme Programming immersion who was so horrified by the use of a non-locking version-control system (CVS) that he walked out of the class on the first day.) ❄ ❄ I’m wary of talking about themes to an event where I attend less than one-tenth of the sessions, but a topic I kept coming across was how large enterprises were embracing this technology - or rather not. One participant used a lovely metaphor: corporations have acquired a Swiss-army knife, but are only using the toothpick. I see plenty of decent reasons for this: it’s one thing for a startup or individual to use a hot technology, but there’s a big difference between a website going down and your factories grinding to a halt. Big organizations involve workflows involving lots of people that have built up over many years - they don’t change easily. Security concerns abound, the lethal trifecta still lurks. In particular good use of AI in enterprises relies on good data, and many such organizations don’t have their data in a decent shape. The path to getting agent-ready data isn’t trivial and it’s hard to see how we can get the knife and saw out until enterprises are much further down that path. One thing that struck me is that there was little conversation about this at Foocamp - a sign of its visibility among the people there. ❄ ❄ I very much enjoyed Foocamp, but events like this are always a mix of excitement and dread. I knew very few of the people there, so it was a great opportunity to get out of my own social bubble. But I also find it nearly impossible to walk up to people I don’t know (or know slightly) and impose my company on them. The great thing about unconferences is that the nature of the sessions make it plausible for someone like me to engage in conversation during them, and begin some tentative links. Also I thank the many folks there who were friendly to me as I casually walked around trying to hide how much I was panicking. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Laurie Voss says today is 1997 On Saturday, Apollo’s chief economist Torsten Slok published No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector. It’s short and it’s blunt: outside of 7 major tech companies, there is no data yet to support a productivity gain that justifies all the money pouring into tech. My position is that he’s half right: are valuations too high? Absolutely. We’re in a bubble, and it’s absolutely going to pop. But does that mean investing in AI is a waste of money? Absolutely not, and using this early data to try and decide that question would be like trying to decide in 1997 whether the Internet was going to pay off. The data just isn’t there yet, because these things take time. I’m not as sure as he is that we can peg today to 1997 rather than 1999, but I agree that this boom bears a lot of resemblance to the dotcom boom (although I think this one is bigger). While many dotcom companies crashed (I always think of pets.com and webvan) he’s right to point out that anyone who invested in Amazon in 1997 did very well. Where might those good investments be this time? if you can build something that proves you got the answer, AI can get the answer much faster than you can, and there are real productivity gains to be had doing that generally.
